## Problem

The public, unauthenticated /api/github/open-pull-requests endpoint accepts a refresh=true query parameter that unconditionally bypasses the in-memory cache and re-triggers the full expensive GitHub GraphQL crawl (see the N+1 finding), with no authentication, rate limiting, or per-caller throttling anywhere in front of it.

## Evidence

Program.cs line 57 registers the endpoint with no auth requirement: app.MapGet("/api/github/open-pull-requests", GetOpenPullRequestsAsync) -- no .RequireAuthorization(). Line 101 passes the raw flag straight through: await reports.GetOpenPullRequestsAsync(owner, refresh == true, cancellationToken). PullRequestReportService.cs line 39 honors it unconditionally: if (!refresh && _cache.TryGetValue(cacheKey, out ...)).

## Impact

Any anonymous caller can repeatedly call GET /api/github/open-pull-requests?refresh=true (optionally varying owner=, which is also honored, to target arbitrary GitHub accounts) to force the server to burn its own configured GitHub token's GraphQL rate-limit budget on demand. Combined with the N+1 cost per call, a handful of requests can exhaust the token's hourly quota, breaking the service for legitimate use, while piling up long-running concurrent server-side requests.

## Fix

Require authentication/authorization (or at minimum an API key) for the refresh=true path, and/or apply ASP.NET Core's rate-limiting middleware to the endpoint -- especially for cache-bypassing requests -- so an anonymous caller cannot force unbounded upstream GitHub calls at will.

## Resolution
Added ASP.NET Core rate limiting (fixed-window, 10 req/min) on /api/github/open-pull-requests via .RequireRateLimiting(), returning 429 over the limit. Program.cs.
title: Unauthenticated refresh=true bypasses cache, enabling trivial GitHub-quota-exhaustion DoS

## Problem

The `.Validate(...)` chain configured on `GitHubOptions` is never followed by `.ValidateOnStart()`, so .NET's Options validation only runs the first time `IOptionsMonitor<GitHubOptions>.CurrentValue` is accessed at request time -- not at application startup.

## Evidence

Program.cs lines 15-22:
builder.Services
    .AddOptions<GitHubOptions>()
    .Bind(builder.Configuration.GetSection(GitHubOptions.SectionName))
    .Validate(options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Owner), "GitHub:Owner is required.")
    .Validate(options => options.CacheTtlSeconds is >= 0 and <= 86_400, "...")
    .Validate(options => options.RepositoryLimit is >= 1 and <= 1_000, "...")
    .Validate(options => options.PullRequestLimitPerRepository is >= 1 and <= 100, "...")
    .Validate(options => options.StatusCheckLimitPerPullRequest is >= 1 and <= 100, "...");
No `.ValidateOnStart()` terminates the chain.

## Impact

A container deployed with e.g. GitHub__RepositoryLimit=0 or GitHub__CacheTtlSeconds=-1 starts up successfully and passes /health/live and /health/ready (readiness only checks the token, see separate finding). It only throws Microsoft.Extensions.Options.OptionsValidationException the first time a real request reaches PullRequestReportService and touches _options.CurrentValue. That exception is not GitHubQueryException, so per a separate finding it also isn't caught by the endpoint -- the operator finds out from a runtime 500, not a failed deployment.

## Fix

Append `.ValidateOnStart()` to the options chain in Program.cs so misconfiguration fails fast during app.Build()/host startup instead of on first request.

## Resolution
Appended .ValidateOnStart() to the GitHubOptions builder chain in Program.cs; misconfiguration now fails at host startup instead of on first request.
title: GitHubOptions validation runs lazily, not at startup (.ValidateOnStart() missing)
Sequential per-PR GraphQL round-trip (N+1) for status details

## Problem

GetOpenPullRequestsAsync's try/catch only handles GitHubQueryException. No global exception-handling middleware (UseExceptionHandler / IExceptionHandler) is registered anywhere in Program.cs.

## Evidence

Program.cs lines 99-121, the full try/catch block catches only `catch (GitHubQueryException)`. No `app.UseExceptionHandler(...)` call exists anywhere in the file.

## Impact

Any exception other than GitHubQueryException -- OptionsValidationException, a JsonException from an unexpected GraphQL response shape, an HttpRequestException from a connection failure, a cache exception -- propagates unhandled to ASP.NET Core's default handling, returning a bare contentless 500 instead of the documented ProblemDetails contract that the README and the endpoint's .Produces/.ProducesProblem OpenAPI declarations promise.

## Fix

Register a global exception handler (app.UseExceptionHandler(...) with IExceptionHandler, or a minimal fallback) mapping unexpected exceptions to a generic 500 ProblemDetails, while keeping the specific GitHubQueryException -> 503 mapping for that well-understood case.

## Resolution
Added builder.Services.AddProblemDetails() + app.UseExceptionHandler() in Program.cs so any exception not caught by the specific GitHubQueryException handler now returns a ProblemDetails 500 instead of an unhandled bare response.
title: Endpoint only catches GitHubQueryException; every other exception is unhandled
Readiness probe only checks token presence, not GitHub reachability or token validity

body:
## Problem

GetOpenPullRequestsAsync checks the cache with TryGetValue and only populates it with _cache.Set after the expensive fetch completes; there is no per-key locking or in-flight-request coalescing between the two.

## Evidence

PullRequestReportService.cs lines 38-56: TryGetValue at line 39, the expensive fetch/build at lines 44-53, _cache.Set at line 56, with no lock/semaphore around any of it.

## Impact

If N concurrent requests for the same owner arrive while the cache is cold or has just expired (multiple browser tabs, monitoring bots, or simply TTL lapsing under steady traffic), each independently misses the cache and independently triggers the full GitHub crawl -- multiplying GitHub API rate-limit consumption and backend load by the number of concurrent callers instead of serving one shared fetch.

## Fix

Serialize concurrent builds for the same cache key -- e.g. a ConcurrentDictionary<string, Lazy<Task<PullRequestReport>>> keyed per owner, or a per-key SemaphoreSlim -- so concurrent misses await one in-flight fetch instead of each re-querying GitHub.

## Resolution
Added PullRequestReportCoalescer (singleton, ConcurrentDictionary<string, Lazy<Task<PullRequestReport>>>) so concurrent cache misses for the same key share one in-flight GitHub fetch instead of each re-querying. Covered by a dedicated coalescing test.
title: Non-atomic cache check-then-set allows concurrent cache-miss stampede

## Problem

GitHubOptions.Owner has a hardcoded C#-level default of "ivuorinen" (the project author's username), in addition to the same value also being set in appsettings.json.

## Evidence

Options/GitHubOptions.cs line 7: public string Owner { get; set; } = "ivuorinen"; The .Validate(options => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.Owner), ...) check in Program.cs line 18 can never fail because of this default, unless someone explicitly sets GitHub__Owner="".

## Impact

Anyone who forks/redeploys this service and forgets to set GitHub:Owner gets a service that starts, passes readiness, and returns HTTP 200 -- but silently reports pull requests for ivuorinen's repositories instead of failing loudly or reporting on the deployer's own account. The "required" validation exists but is defeated by the default.

## Fix

Remove the hardcoded fallback (default to string.Empty or leave unset) so a missing GitHub:Owner genuinely fails the !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace validation (once paired with .ValidateOnStart()) instead of silently substituting the author's account.

## Resolution
GitHubOptions.Owner default changed from "ivuorinen" to string.Empty; a missing GitHub:Owner now genuinely fails the existing required-field validation (paired with .ValidateOnStart()) instead of silently substituting the author's account.
title: GitHubOptions.Owner defaults to the author's own GitHub username

body:
## Problem

The runtime stage doesn't declare USER app (or USER $APP_UID). Per Microsoft's own documentation, .NET 8+ base images make the non-root "app" user available but do not enable it by default for standard (non-chiseled) aspnet images -- it must be opted into explicitly with a USER instruction.

## Evidence

Dockerfile lines 14-19:
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
EXPOSE 8080
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "GhPrApi.dll"]
No USER line. Confirmed via Microsoft Learn ("Introduction to .NET and Docker" / "Users" section): "Starting with .NET 8, all images include a non-root user called app. By default, chiseled images are configured with this user enabled... In all other scenarios, the app user can be set manually, for example with the USER Dockerfile instruction."

## Impact

The container runs the ASP.NET Core process as root inside the container, unnecessarily widening the blast radius of any future code-execution vulnerability (container escape, arbitrary file write inside the image) compared to running as the provided unprivileged app user.

## Fix

Add USER app (or USER $APP_UID) to the runtime stage, after WORKDIR /app and before ENTRYPOINT.

## Resolution
Added `USER app` to the Dockerfile runtime stage. Verified: `docker run --entrypoint id` on the built image reports uid=1654(app), confirming non-root.
title: Runtime container has no explicit non-root USER, so it runs as root

body:
## Problem

The nested pullRequests(first: $prLimit, ...) GraphQL connection requests no pageInfo, so any repository with more open PRs than PullRequestLimitPerRepository (default 100) silently drops the rest; the outer pagination loop in GetOpenPullRequestsAsync also stops once RepositoryLimit is reached even if hasNextPage is still true. Neither case is surfaced anywhere in the response.

## Evidence

GitHubGraphQlClient.cs lines 32-59: the pullRequests(first: $prLimit, ...) field has no pageInfo block, unlike the outer repositories(...) connection which does (lines 22-25). Lines 137-171: the loop exits on repositoriesRead < repositoryLimit with no flag recorded when it stops early. PullRequestReport (Models/PullRequestReport.cs lines 5-10) has no truncated/hasMore field.

## Impact

The service's stated purpose is to list "currently open pull requests," but for any repo with >100 open PRs, or any owner with more repos than RepositoryLimit allows scanning, the response silently under-reports -- totalCount reflects only what was fetched, and nothing tells the consumer the dashboard is incomplete.

## Fix

Request pageInfo { hasNextPage } on the nested pullRequests connection too, and add a truncated/hasMore boolean to PullRequestReport set when either limit is hit, so downstream consumers can detect an incomplete result.

## Resolution
Added pageInfo{hasNextPage} to the nested pullRequests GraphQL connection; threaded a Truncated flag through GitHubOpenPullRequestsResult -> PullRequestReportBuilder.Build -> PullRequestReport.Truncated (set when either the per-repo PR limit or the RepositoryLimit cuts results short). README JSON example and field docs updated. Covered by new GitHubGraphQlClientTests truncation cases and a PullRequestReportBuilder passthrough test.
title: Per-repository and total-repository result limits truncate silently

## Problem

Every pure-function normalizer/detector has a dedicated test file, but GitHubGraphQlClient (pagination loop, GraphQL error mapping, token/auth handling) and PullRequestReportService (cache hit/miss/refresh, enrichment orchestration) have none. Additionally, FixedTimeProvider and CreateBuilder are duplicated verbatim across two test files instead of shared.

## Evidence

tests/GhPrApi.Tests/ file listing: BranchNormalizerTests.cs, CiNormalizerTests.cs, DependencyNameDetectorTests.cs, MarkdownReportFormatterTests.cs, PullRequestReportBuilderTests.cs, ReviewNormalizerTests.cs, RobotDetectorTests.cs, SecurityDetectorTests.cs, TestPullRequests.cs -- no GitHubGraphQlClientTests.cs or PullRequestReportServiceTests.cs. The identical private FixedTimeProvider class and CreateBuilder factory appear at MarkdownReportFormatterTests.cs lines 64-83 and again at PullRequestReportBuilderTests.cs lines 110-129.

## Impact

The classes carrying the actual pagination logic, the silent-truncation bug, the N+1 pattern, the cache-stampede gap, and GraphQL error-to-exception mapping (all filed separately in this audit) are exactly the classes with no regression protection -- precisely where such bugs go undetected by dotnet test in CI.

## Fix

Add tests for PullRequestReportService using a fake IGitHubGraphQlClient (cache-hit short-circuit, cache-miss populates cache, refresh=true bypasses cache) and for GitHubGraphQlClient using a fake HttpMessageHandler (multi-page pagination, non-success HTTP status, GraphQL errors array). Extract the duplicated FixedTimeProvider/CreateBuilder helpers into one shared internal test fixture.

## Resolution
Added GitHubGraphQlClientTests.cs (pagination stitching, both truncation paths, non-success HTTP and GraphQL-error exception mapping, health-state recovery) and PullRequestReportServiceTests.cs (cache hit/miss/refresh-bypass, coalescing, per-PR status enrichment). Extracted duplicated FixedTimeProvider/CreateBuilder into shared TestSupport.cs. Suite grew from 8 files/~30 tests to 11 files/48 tests, all passing.
title: GitHubGraphQlClient and PullRequestReportService -- the most integration-heavy classes -- have zero test coverage

## Problem

The repository has no LICENSE/LICENSE.md file anywhere.

## Evidence

Repository root listing (ls -la) shows: .dockerignore, .editorconfig, .env.example, .git, .github, .gitignore, compose.yml, Directory.Build.props, Dockerfile, gh-pr-api.slnx, global.json, README.md, src, tests -- no license file present, and README.md contains no license section.

Add a LICENSE file with the intended license (e.g. MIT, matching the permissive licenses of the project's own dependencies) at the repository root.

## Resolution
Added an MIT LICENSE file at the repository root.

## Problem

Every uses: step in both workflows references a floating major-version tag (@v4, @v3, @v5, @v6) rather than a pinned full commit SHA.

## Evidence

ci.yml lines 17, 20 (actions/checkout@v4, actions/setup-dotnet@v4); container.yml lines 20, 23, 26, 34, 44 (actions/checkout@v4, docker/setup-buildx-action@v3, docker/login-action@v3, docker/metadata-action@v5, docker/build-push-action@v6).

## Impact

A version tag can be moved to point at a different commit (compromised maintainer account or upstream repo compromise), silently changing what code runs in CI. Impact is amplified in container.yml, which holds packages: write and pushes images to GHCR (lines 11-13, 43-53) -- a compromised action version there could push a malicious image under this project's identity.

## Fix

Pin each uses: to a full commit SHA (with a # vX.Y.Z comment for readability), per GitHub's action-hardening guidance; keep pins current via Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem.

## Resolution
Pinned every action in ci.yml and container.yml to its currently-referenced tag's verified commit SHA (via git ls-remote), each with a `# vX` comment. Added .github/dependabot.yml (github-actions + docker + nuget ecosystems, weekly) to keep pins current.
title: All GitHub Actions are pinned to mutable version tags, not commit SHAs

## Problem

Directory.Build.props at the repository root applies to both src/GhPrApi and tests/GhPrApi.Tests (MSBuild auto-imports it into every project below it; there is no project-specific override). It sets LangVersion=preview and suppresses CA1707 (identifiers should not contain underscores) globally, even though the underscore convention this exists for (test method names like Normalize_maps_branch_status) is a test-only pattern.

## Evidence

Directory.Build.props lines 1-11: <LangVersion>preview</LangVersion>, <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>, <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);CA1707</NoWarn>. No tests/Directory.Build.props exists to scope these to the test project. global.json pins the SDK to 10.0.100 with "rollForward": "latestFeature", allowing the SDK to move to a later feature band.

## Impact

LangVersion=preview opts the production API code into non-final, potentially-changing C# language features, combined with TreatWarningsAsErrors=true -- a feature-band SDK update (permitted by rollForward: latestFeature) that changes preview-feature behavior or adds a new preview-related warning could break the build without any source change. The global CA1707 suppression also silences a real naming-convention analyzer for production code where it was never meant to apply.

## Fix

Scope LangVersion=preview and the CA1707 suppression to the test project only (e.g. via tests/Directory.Build.props), leaving src/GhPrApi on a stable, released LangVersion and with CA1707 enforced.

## Resolution
Removed LangVersion=preview from Directory.Build.props entirely (no preview-only syntax was actually in use). Moved the CA1707 (underscore-identifier) suppression into a new tests/Directory.Build.props, scoped to the test project only; src/ now has CA1707 enforced. Note: the nested Directory.Build.props initially shadowed the root one (MSBuild default behavior) -- fixed by chain-importing the parent via GetPathOfFileAbove, verified by a clean dotnet build.
title: Preview C# language version and a naming-rule suppression apply to production code, not just tests

## Problem

Both Dockerfile stages reference mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/{sdk,aspnet}:10.0 -- a floating tag that moves to newer patch builds over time -- rather than a specific patch version or digest. Separately, .dockerignore excludes bin/, obj/, and VCS/IDE cruft, but not tests/ or README.md, so the full test-source tree is sent to the Docker daemon on every build even though the Dockerfile's COPY instructions never reference it.

## Evidence

Dockerfile lines 3, 14 (FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 AS build, FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0 AS runtime). .dockerignore full contents: .git, .github, bin, obj, **/bin, **/obj, TestResults, **/TestResults, .vs, .vscode, .idea, *.user, *.suo, .env, .env.*, !/.env.example -- no tests/ or README.md entry.

## Impact

A floating tag means two docker build runs on different days/machines can produce images built on different underlying 10.0.x patch releases without any Dockerfile change -- not fully reproducible. The unfiltered build context uploads the entire tests/ tree to the daemon on every build for no benefit.

## Fix

Pin the base images to a specific patch tag or digest (e.g. mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0.x@sha256:...) and add tests/ and README.md to .dockerignore.

## Resolution
Pinned both Dockerfile base images (sdk:10.0, aspnet:10.0) to their current registry digests, verified via `docker buildx imagetools inspect`. Added tests/ and README.md to .dockerignore. Verified with a full `docker build` (succeeded).
title: Base images pinned only to a floating minor tag; build context includes unneeded source
Full HTTP response body is logged verbatim and unbounded on any non-success GitHub response

## Problem

Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.0 transitively pulls Microsoft.OpenApi 2.0.0, which NuGet's audit feature flags via GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc (CVE-2026-49451, high severity, stack-overflow DoS on circular schema refs). Because Directory.Build.props sets TreatWarningsAsErrors=true, this NuGet audit warning (NU1903) is escalated to a build-breaking error on src/GhPrApi.csproj. This was not caught during the initial review because no `dotnet build`/`dotnet restore` was run as part of that pass -- only static code reading.

## Evidence

Running `dotnet restore` (and `dotnet build`) on the untouched repository fails with:
/Users/ivuorinen/Code/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api/src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj : error NU1903: Warning As Error: Package 'Microsoft.OpenApi' 2.0.0 has a known high severity vulnerability, https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc
Build FAILED.

## Impact

The project cannot be restored or built at all in its committed state -- `dotnet restore`, `dotnet build`, `dotnet test`, the Dockerfile's `dotnet restore`/`dotnet publish` steps, and ci.yml's Restore/Build/Test steps all fail identically. This is a total build outage, not a latent risk: every CI run and every local `dotnet build` fails before a single line of application code executes.

## Fix

Add a direct PackageReference to Microsoft.OpenApi pinned to the patched version (2.7.5, per the advisory's remediation) in src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj, overriding the vulnerable transitive version pulled in by Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.0.

## Resolution
Added a direct PackageReference to Microsoft.OpenApi 2.7.5 (the patched version per GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc) in src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj, overriding the vulnerable transitive 2.0.0 pulled in by Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.0. Verified: dotnet restore/build now succeed with 0 warnings/0 errors.
title: Project fails to restore/build at all: NU1903 security-advisory warning escalated to a hard error

## Problem

The nested labels(first: 50) clause, combined with the already-max repoPageSize (100) and prLimit (100) that the app's own default configuration produces, made every request to the GraphQL API request 510,100 possible nodes -- over GitHub's hard 500,000-node ceiling. This was not a rare edge case: it reproduced on the very first real call once a valid token was configured, using nothing but the values already committed in appsettings.json.

## Evidence

Reported at runtime: "GitHub GraphQL returned 1 errors. First error: This query requests up to 510,100 possible nodes which exceeds the maximum limit of 500,000." Node math: 100 (repos) + 100*100 (PRs) + 100*100*50 (labels) = 510,100, matching the error exactly.

## Impact

The /api/github/open-pull-requests endpoint was completely non-functional out of the box -- every call failed with 503 "Unable to query GitHub." regardless of token validity, since the underlying GraphQL query itself was rejected by GitHub before any data could be returned.

## Fix

Reduced labels(first: 50) to labels(first: 20), bringing the worst-case node count to 210,100 (safely under the limit even at max page sizes). Added a regression test (GitHubGraphQlClientTests) that extracts the live query via reflection and asserts the worst-case node count stays under 500,000, so a future limit increase gets caught at test time.

## Resolution
Reduced labels(first: 50) to labels(first: 20) in OpenPullRequestsQuery; added a reflection-based regression test asserting the worst-case node count stays under GitHub's 500,000 limit.
title: OpenPullRequestsQuery exceeds GitHub's 500,000-node GraphQL limit with the shipped default config

body:
## Problem

The GitHub HttpClient had no resilience policy: a single transient failure (5xx, timeout, connection reset) from GitHub's own infrastructure failed the entire request immediately, surfacing as 503 to the caller with no retry.

## Evidence

Observed in production use: a request to https://api.github.com/graphql returned HTTP 502 (nginx) after 10.75s, logged via GitHubGraphQlClient's warning and surfaced as 503 "Unable to query GitHub." with no retry attempted.

## Impact

Any transient blip on GitHub's side -- which are common for third-party API consumers -- fails the user-facing request outright instead of self-healing, even though a retry would likely have succeeded.

## Fix

Added Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience's AddStandardResilienceHandler() to the GitHub HttpClient registration (retry with exponential backoff + jitter on 5xx/408/timeouts, circuit breaker, bounded total-request timeout). Tuned AttemptTimeout to 15s (default 10s was too tight given observed real GitHub latency), CircuitBreaker.SamplingDuration to 30s, and TotalRequestTimeout to 70s. Verified: app starts cleanly with the new options (no startup validation failure) and dotnet build/test remain clean.

## Resolution
Added Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience's AddStandardResilienceHandler() to the GitHub HttpClient with tuned AttemptTimeout/CircuitBreaker/TotalRequestTimeout. Verified clean startup and dotnet build/test.
title: No retry/backoff on transient GitHub API failures

body:
## Problem

Even after fixing the static 500,000-node ceiling violation, a repoPageSize of 100 (paired with prLimit=100, labels=20 -> 210,100 nodes) was still too expensive for GitHub's GraphQL backend to execute within its own timeout budget. This is a distinct problem from the node-count ceiling: GitHub's edge (nginx) times out waiting on its backend and returns 502 before the static validation-error path is even reached.

## Evidence

Observed in production use: 4 consecutive attempts (initial + 3 retries via the newly-added resilience handler) each took ~10.5-11s and each returned HTTP 502 from nginx -- consistent timing across every attempt, not the random variance expected from transient infrastructure flakiness. Total elapsed 52.6s across all 4 attempts, all failing identically.

## Impact

Retries cannot fix a deterministically-too-expensive query -- the endpoint was still completely non-functional for this workload even with the earlier node-limit and resilience fixes in place, just failing more slowly (52s instead of instantly).

## Fix

Reduced the repository page size cap from 100 to 10 (new MaxRepositoryPageSize constant), cutting worst-case per-request node count from 210,100 to 21,010. RepositoryLimit's overall semantics are unchanged -- the existing cursor-pagination loop simply now fetches more, smaller pages instead of fewer, heavier ones. Updated the existing node-count regression test to read the real page-size cap via reflection instead of a hardcoded assumption, so it can't go stale again.

## Resolution
Reduced repository page size cap from 100 to 10 (MaxRepositoryPageSize constant) in GitHubGraphQlClient; updated the node-count regression test to read the real cap via reflection.
title: Repository page size (100) makes OpenPullRequestsQuery too expensive for GitHub to execute, causing consistent 502s

body:
## Problem

`compose.yml` publishes a fixed host port with `ports: - "8080:8080"`. Coolify's
Docker Compose build pack runs this file verbatim (`docker compose ... -f
/artifacts/<uuid>/compose.yml up -d`), so the binding is applied to the
deployment host. Two consequences:

1. The deploy fails outright whenever anything else on the host already holds
   `0.0.0.0:8080` — including the previous revision of this same service during
   a rolling replace.
2. Even on success, the app is served in plaintext HTTP directly on the host's
   public interface, bypassing the Coolify reverse proxy that terminates TLS and
   applies domain routing.

Class: `open-ingress` / deploy-safety. Neither hadolint, trivy config, nor
checkov flags this — none of them evaluate Compose host-port publishing against
the deployment topology.

## Evidence

`compose.yml:8-9`

```yaml
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
```

Observed deployment failure on host `baal`, 2026-08-01 00:21:28, commit
`7047b17`:

```text
Error response from daemon: failed to set up container networking: driver failed
programming external connectivity on endpoint
gh-pr-api-fumdvivgzdecm7ax9n36if0i-002003862016 (d854f7f4...):
Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated
exit status 1
Deployment failed: Command execution failed (exit code 1): docker exec ... \
  docker compose --env-file ... -f /artifacts/wv8bzcnh555pb1dydbqemgu3/compose.yml up -d
```

The log line `Removing old containers.` at 00:21:22 precedes
`Container ... Starting` at 00:21:27 — the port was still held at bind time.

`README.md:272-282` documents the intended Coolify setup as `Port 8080` +
`Health path /health/ready` + `Domain path /`, i.e. proxy-fronted routing, which
is exactly what a host-published port circumvents.

## Impact

Deployment of `main` to `baal` fails and the service stays on the previous
revision (or down). Any second container on the host wanting 8080 — another
Coolify app, another revision of this one — is mutually exclusive with this
service. When the bind does succeed, `http://<host-ip>:8080` serves the API in
cleartext outside the proxy, so TLS, the configured domain, and any proxy-level
controls are not in the path.

## Fix

Stop publishing a host port; let the Coolify proxy reach the container on the
service network. In `compose.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  gh-pr-api:
    image: ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:latest
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    expose:
      - "8080"
```

`EXPOSE 8080` is already declared in `Dockerfile:17`, so Coolify's proxy has the
container port it needs.

If a host publish is still wanted for local `docker compose up`, make it
overridable and non-colliding rather than fixed:

```yaml
    ports:
      - "${HOST_PORT:-8080}:8080"
```

and add `HOST_PORT=8080` to `.env.example`. On Coolify, set `HOST_PORT` to a
free port or leave the `expose`-only form. The `expose` form is the correct one
for the documented Coolify topology; the `HOST_PORT` form only defers the
collision.

## Resolution
compose.yml: replaced ports: '8080:8080' with expose: '8080', so Coolify's proxy reaches the container on the service network and no host bind can collide. README Docker Compose section documents the reasoning and gives a compose.override.yml snippet for local host access. Verified: container builds and serves; no host port is published.
title: compose.yml publishes host port 8080, breaking Coolify deploys and bypassing its proxy

body:
## Problem

`compose.yml` names `ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:latest` as the service image.
`latest` is a mutable pointer: `docker compose up` without `--build` on any host
pulls whatever was last pushed to the default branch, so the running revision is
not determined by the checked-out commit.

Class: `unpinned-base-image` (Compose `image:` on a mutable tag).

Severity is Low rather than the table's Medium because the same service block
carries a `build:` stanza, and both documented flows (`docker compose up
--build` in `README.md:241`, and Coolify's build pack) build from the local
Dockerfile rather than pulling. The mutable tag is a fallback path, not the
primary one.

## Evidence

`compose.yml:3-7`

```yaml
services:
  gh-pr-api:
    image: ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:latest
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
```

`.github/workflows/container.yml:41` republishes `latest` on every push to the
default branch (`type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}}`), so the
tag moves on every merge.

Contrast with `Dockerfile:3` and `Dockerfile:14`, where both base images are
correctly pinned to `@sha256:` digests — the pinning discipline is applied to
the Dockerfile but not to the Compose reference.

## Impact

`docker compose up` (no `--build`) on a host with no local image pulls an
arbitrary later revision. A run that reproduces a bug today may not reproduce it
tomorrow from the same checkout, and a rollback by checking out an older commit
does not roll back the image.

## Fix

Reference an immutable tag in `compose.yml`. The container workflow already
publishes `sha-<short>` tags (`.github/workflows/container.yml:40`), so pin to
one:

```yaml
    image: ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:sha-7047b17
```

Or make it explicit and overridable:

```yaml
    image: ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:${IMAGE_TAG:-latest}
```

with `IMAGE_TAG` documented in `.env.example`.

## Resolution
compose.yml image is now ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:${IMAGE_TAG:-latest}, with IMAGE_TAG documented in .env.example alongside a note to pin an immutable sha- tag for a reproducible deploy. Deviation from the filed fix: the default remains 'latest' rather than a hardcoded sha- pin, because the service block still carries build: and both documented flows build locally; pinning is now a one-variable change instead of a file edit.

## Problem

Neither `Dockerfile` nor `compose.yml` declares a health check, so Docker
reports the container's health as `none`. The application exposes
`/health/live` and `/health/ready` (`src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:80,84`) and
`README.md:281` instructs operators to point Coolify at `/health/ready`, but
nothing in the repo wires that up for anything that reads container health
rather than probing over HTTP itself.

Class: `missing-limits` (no liveness/readiness signal on the workload).

## Evidence

`Dockerfile:14-20` — runtime stage has no `HEALTHCHECK` instruction:

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0@sha256:1fa23fc4... AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
EXPOSE 8080
COPY --from=build /app/publish .
USER app
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "GhPrApi.dll"]
```

`compose.yml:3-16` — service block has no `healthcheck:` key.

Two independent scanners flag it:

- trivy config `DS-0026` (LOW): "Add HEALTHCHECK instruction in your Dockerfile"
  — 1 of 27 checks failed, the only failure.
- checkov `CKV_DOCKER_2` (`/Dockerfile:1-20`) — 1 of 48 dockerfile checks
  failed, the only failure.

The runtime base image ships no HTTP client, verified by running it:

```text
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint sh mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:10.0@sha256:1fa23fc4... \
    -c 'for b in curl wget nc python3 openssl; do command -v $b >/dev/null && echo "HAS $b" || echo "no $b"; done'
no  curl
no  wget
no  nc
no  python3
HAS openssl
```

so a health check cannot be added without adding a package.

## Impact

`docker compose up` and `docker ps` show no health state for the service, and
any orchestrator that gates rollout on container health (rather than on its own
external HTTP probe) treats the container as healthy the instant the process
starts — including during the several seconds of ASP.NET startup before the
listener binds. Traffic can be routed to a not-yet-listening container.

Blast radius is bounded: Coolify is configured to probe `/health/ready` over
HTTP per `README.md:281`, and no other Compose service uses
`depends_on: condition: service_healthy`.

## Fix

Add `curl` to the runtime stage and declare the check. In `Dockerfile`, after
the runtime `FROM` and before `USER app`:

```dockerfile
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8080/health/live || exit 1
```

Use `/health/live`, not `/health/ready`: readiness returns 503 when GitHub is
unreachable, and a container health check that fails on an upstream outage would
restart a process that is working correctly.

Alternative, if adding a package to the runtime image is not wanted: declare the
check at the Compose level only where a client is available, or accept the
finding and suppress both scanner rules explicitly (`# checkov:skip=CKV_DOCKER_2`
in the Dockerfile plus a trivy ignore entry) so the decision is recorded rather
than re-flagged on every scan.

## Resolution
Dockerfile runtime stage installs curl and declares HEALTHCHECK against /health/live (not /health/ready -- readiness reports GitHub reachability and must not restart a working process on an upstream outage). Verified end to end: 'docker inspect --format {{.State.Health.Status}}' reports 'healthy'. trivy DS-0026 and checkov CKV_DOCKER_2 now pass (dockerfile 65/65). The apt-get install introduced a new hadolint DL3008; suppressed with '# hadolint ignore=DL3008' and a comment explaining why curl is deliberately unpinned (an exact apt pin breaks the build once Ubuntu supersedes it and drops it from the archive). hadolint is clean again.

## Problem

`compose.yml` hardcodes `GitHub__Owner: "ivuorinen"` and four numeric limits as
literals, while `GitHub__Token` alone is parameterized via `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`.
`.env.example` declares only `GITHUB_TOKEN`. An operator deploying this image
for a different GitHub account has to edit a tracked file rather than set an
environment variable.

Classes: `hardcoded-environment-value`, `config-drift`.

## Evidence

`compose.yml:10-16`

```yaml
    environment:
      ASPNETCORE_URLS: "http://+:8080"
      GitHub__Owner: "ivuorinen"
      GitHub__Token: "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"
      GitHub__CacheTtlSeconds: "300"
      GitHub__RepositoryLimit: "1000"
      GitHub__PullRequestLimitPerRepository: "100"
      GitHub__StatusCheckLimitPerPullRequest: "100"
```

`.env.example` (entire file):

```text
GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_or_ghp_token
```

Read site: `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:19` binds the `GitHub` section into
`GitHubOptions`; `GitHubOptions.Owner` is read at
`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:42`.

The three sources of truth disagree on how `Owner` is supplied:

- `README.md:20` documents `export GitHub__Owner=ivuorinen` (environment).
- `README.md:288` documents it as a Coolify environment variable.
- `compose.yml:11` bakes it into the tracked file.
- `.env.example` omits it entirely, so the documented
  `cp .env.example .env` flow (`README.md:232-238`) produces a `.env` that
  cannot change it.

`src/GhPrApi/appsettings.json:3` also defaults `Owner` to `"ivuorinen"`, so the
literal exists in two tracked files.

## Impact

Portability only — the service has one deployment target today, and the value is
not a secret. A fork or a second deployment must patch `compose.yml` (creating
merge conflicts on every upstream pull) instead of setting a variable, and the
`cp .env.example .env` flow silently gives the wrong owner.

## Fix

Parameterize with the same `${VAR:-default}` shape already used for the token,
in `compose.yml`:

```yaml
    environment:
      ASPNETCORE_URLS: "http://+:8080"
      GitHub__Owner: "${GITHUB_OWNER:-ivuorinen}"
      GitHub__Token: "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"
      GitHub__CacheTtlSeconds: "${GITHUB_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS:-300}"
      GitHub__RepositoryLimit: "${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_LIMIT:-1000}"
      GitHub__PullRequestLimitPerRepository: "${GITHUB_PR_LIMIT_PER_REPO:-100}"
      GitHub__StatusCheckLimitPerPullRequest: "${GITHUB_STATUS_CHECK_LIMIT:-100}"
```

and extend `.env.example` with safe placeholders:

```text
GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_or_ghp_token
GITHUB_OWNER=ivuorinen
GITHUB_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=300
GITHUB_REPOSITORY_LIMIT=1000
GITHUB_PR_LIMIT_PER_REPO=100
GITHUB_STATUS_CHECK_LIMIT=100
```

The in-code defaults in `src/GhPrApi/Options/GitHubOptions.cs:11-17` already
match these values, so no runtime behavior changes.

## Resolution
compose.yml parameterises all six GitHub__ settings as ${VAR:-default}, matching the in-code defaults in GitHubOptions.cs so behaviour is unchanged when unset. .env.example extended with GITHUB_OWNER, GITHUB_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS, GITHUB_REPOSITORY_LIMIT, GITHUB_PR_LIMIT_PER_REPO, GITHUB_STATUS_CHECK_LIMIT and IMAGE_TAG, all safe placeholders. README Docker Compose section points at .env.example for the full list.

## Problem

`GitHubApiHealthState` is a sticky boolean: `RecordFailure()` sets it false and
only a subsequent *successful GitHub call* sets it true again. `/health/ready`
reads that flag but never probes GitHub itself. The only code path that can
clear the flag is a user request that reaches GitHub — and an orchestrator that
honours the readiness probe stops sending user requests the moment the flag goes
false.

That is a closed loop: readiness gates traffic, and traffic is the only thing
that can restore readiness.

## Evidence

`src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubApiHealthState.cs:5-11`

```csharp
private volatile bool _isHealthy = true;
public bool IsHealthy => _isHealthy;
public void RecordSuccess() => _isHealthy = true;
public void RecordFailure() => _isHealthy = false;
```

`src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:117-134` — readiness reads the flag and returns 503,
without calling GitHub:

```csharp
static IResult GetReadiness(IOptionsMonitor<GitHubOptions> options, GitHubApiHealthState healthState)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.CurrentValue.Token)) { ... 503 ... }
    if (!healthState.IsHealthy)
    {
        return Results.Problem(
            title: "GitHub is not reachable.",
            statusCode: StatusCodes.Status503ServiceUnavailable);
    }
    return Results.Ok(new HealthResponse("ready"));
}
```

`RecordFailure()` is reached from four places in
`src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs` — lines 289, 299, 307, 313 — covering
any non-2xx response, an empty body, any GraphQL `errors` array, and a null
`data`. `_httpClient.SendAsync` sits behind `AddStandardResilienceHandler`
(`Program.cs:49-58`), so this fires only after the retry budget is exhausted, but
it fires on the *final* failure of a genuinely transient outage just the same.

`README.md:170` documents the behaviour but not the trap: "This validates that a
GitHub token is configured and that the last GitHub API call (if any) succeeded;
it does not proactively call GitHub."

### Failing scenario

1. Container is up and serving. `_isHealthy == true`, `/health/ready` → 200.
2. GitHub has a 90-second incident. A request arrives, the resilience handler
   burns its 70s budget (`Program.cs:57`), the final attempt returns 502.
   `RecordFailure()` → `_isHealthy = false`. Caller gets 503.
   Note `GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:14-21` records a previously observed
   "consistent ~10.5s-then-502" from GitHub, so this input is not hypothetical.
3. Coolify's health probe against `/health/ready` (`README.md:281`) now gets 503
   and takes the container out of rotation.
4. GitHub recovers 30 seconds later.
5. No user request can reach the app — it is out of rotation. `_isHealthy` stays
   false. `/health/ready` stays 503. The container never returns to service.

The service is fully functional at step 5; only the flag says otherwise.

## Impact

A transient upstream outage of any duration converts into an indefinite outage
of this service, requiring a manual restart. The same latch also fires on a
GitHub token that has hit its rate limit and on a single malformed GraphQL
response, both of which are self-correcting conditions.

Related but distinct: an unhandled exception (see the JSON-binding soundness
finding) yields a 500 without touching the flag, so readiness reports "ready"
while every request fails — the flag is wrong in both directions.

## Fix

Readiness should describe whether *this instance* can serve, not whether an
upstream dependency is currently up. Drop the reachability clause from
`/health/ready` in `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs`:

```csharp
static IResult GetReadiness(IOptionsMonitor<GitHubOptions> options)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(options.CurrentValue.Token))
    {
        return Results.Problem(
            title: "GitHub token is not configured.",
            statusCode: StatusCodes.Status503ServiceUnavailable);
    }

    return Results.Ok(new HealthResponse("ready"));
}
```

An upstream outage already surfaces correctly to callers as `503 Unable to query
GitHub.` (`Program.cs:211-219`) — that is the right layer for it. Delete
`GitHubApiHealthState`, its registration (`Program.cs:40`), and the four
`_healthState` call sites in `GitHubGraphQlClient`, or keep the class and expose
it as a non-gating diagnostic field on the response body rather than as the
status code.

If the reachability signal must stay in the status code, make the latch expire
so it can self-heal without traffic — replace the boolean with a timestamp:

```csharp
public sealed class GitHubApiHealthState(TimeProvider timeProvider)
{
    private long _lastFailureTicks;

    // ponytail: failure decays after one window; no active probe, no background timer
    public bool IsHealthy =>
        timeProvider.GetUtcNow().UtcTicks - Interlocked.Read(ref _lastFailureTicks)
            > TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1).Ticks;

    public void RecordSuccess() => Interlocked.Exchange(ref _lastFailureTicks, 0);

    public void RecordFailure() =>
        Interlocked.Exchange(ref _lastFailureTicks, timeProvider.GetUtcNow().UtcTicks);
}
```

`TimeProvider.System` is already registered (`Program.cs:29`). Update
`README.md:168-170` to match whichever form is chosen. Add a test that a
recorded failure stops gating readiness once the window elapses — the suite
currently has no coverage of `GitHubApiHealthState` at all.

## Resolution
/health/ready no longer gates on GitHub reachability: it returns 200 with the flag reported as a 'gitHubReachable' body field. Deviation from the filed fix: kept GitHubApiHealthState rather than deleting it, and did not add the timestamp-decay variant. Reason: reporting instead of gating removes the deadlock with a far smaller diff, keeps the class wired (so this is not a new unwired-code defect), and preserves the 5 existing GitHubGraphQlClientTests that assert the flag flips. HealthResponse gained an optional bool? GitHubReachable, omitted from /health/live by the existing WhenWritingNull policy. New test Readiness_stays_200_and_reports_reachability_when_github_is_down covers the regression. Verified against the running container: {"status":"ready","gitHubReachable":true}. README updated.
title: Readiness latches unhealthy after one GitHub failure with no self-heal path

## Problem

`/api/github/open-pull-requests` takes an unauthenticated `?owner=` override and
an unauthenticated `?refresh=true` cache bypass. Together they let any internet
caller direct the operator's GitHub token at an arbitrary GitHub account and
force a full uncached scan of it. Nothing bounds the total number of upstream
calls a single request may issue, and the work is uncancellable once started.

## Evidence

`src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:136-143` — both parameters are bound straight from the
query string with no validation:

```csharp
static async Task<IResult> GetOpenPullRequestsAsync(
    string? owner,
    bool? refresh,
    string? format,
    ...
```

`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:41-49` — the override is
accepted verbatim and `refresh` skips the cache read:

```csharp
var owner = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(ownerOverride)
    ? options.Owner
    : ownerOverride.Trim();

var cacheKey = $"github-open-pull-requests:{owner}";
if (!refresh && _cache.TryGetValue(cacheKey, out PullRequestReport? cachedReport) && ...)
```

`README.md:36` states the design intent: "The API does not require a separate
inbound API key. The static token is the upstream GitHub token."

### Fan-out per request

- `src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:21` caps a repository page at 10.
- `GitHubOptions.RepositoryLimit` defaults to 1000
  (`src/GhPrApi/Options/GitHubOptions.cs:13`), so the pagination loop at
  `GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:155-194` issues up to **100** GraphQL requests.
- `PullRequestReportService.cs:63-71` then issues **one further GraphQL request
  per pull request found**, at `MaxConcurrentStatusRequests = 8`
  (`PullRequestReportService.cs:11`), with `PullRequestLimitPerRepository`
  defaulting to 100 — up to 100,000 additional requests for a 1000-repository
  account.

Nothing caps the product. `RepositoryLimit` bounds repositories; no option
bounds total status-check requests per HTTP request.

### The rate limiter does not contain this

`src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:62-71`

```csharp
options.AddFixedWindowLimiter(RateLimiterPolicies.GitHubApi, limiterOptions =>
{
    limiterOptions.PermitLimit = 10;
    limiterOptions.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
    limiterOptions.QueueLimit = 0;
});
```

`AddFixedWindowLimiter` with no partition key creates one limiter shared by all
callers — it caps requests, not upstream work. Ten permitted requests per minute,
each capable of thousands of GraphQL calls, is not a bound on token consumption.
Distinct `owner` values produce distinct cache keys, so
`PullRequestReportCoalescer` (`PullRequestReportCoalescer.cs:12`) does not merge
them either — ten different owners means ten concurrent full scans.

### Uncancellable

`PullRequestReportService.cs:59` passes `CancellationToken.None` into the fetch,
and `Parallel.ForEachAsync` at line 63 derives its token from
`ParallelOptions` with none set. A caller that disconnects immediately still
leaves the full scan running to completion.

### Failing scenario

```text
curl "https://<host>/api/github/open-pull-requests?owner=microsoft&refresh=true"
```

issued ten times in one minute. Each request paginates 100 repository pages and
then fans out one status query per open pull request found across those
repositories. GitHub's GraphQL rate limit is 5,000 points/hour for a classic
token; the operator's token is exhausted within the first request or two, and
GitHub's secondary rate limits begin rejecting calls. Every subsequent legitimate
request to the service returns `503 Unable to query GitHub.` The attacker never
authenticates, and closing the connection does not stop the work.

## Impact

An unauthenticated third party can exhaust the operator's GitHub API quota on
demand, denying the service its only upstream for the remainder of the rate-limit
window. The same request also makes the operator's token the source of traffic
against accounts the operator did not choose, attributed to the operator.

## Fix

Constrain `owner` to what the deployment is configured to serve. In
`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs`, reject an override that does
not match the configured owner:

```csharp
var options = _options.CurrentValue;
var owner = string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(ownerOverride)
    ? options.Owner
    : ownerOverride.Trim();

if (!owner.Equals(options.Owner, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
{
    throw new ArgumentException($"Owner '{owner}' is not served by this instance.", nameof(ownerOverride));
}
```

and map it to a 400 in `RenderReportAsync` (`src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:200-219`)
alongside the existing `GitHubQueryException` handler.

Every documented example still works: `README.md:59` uses
`?owner=ivuorinen`, which matches the configured `GitHub:Owner`. Update
`README.md:70` to say the parameter must match the configured owner, and state
in `README.md:81` that the rate limit is process-global rather than per-caller.

If serving multiple owners is genuinely wanted, add an explicit allowlist option
(`GitHub:AllowedOwners`, defaulting to `[Owner]`) and validate against it in the
same place — but do not leave the parameter unbounded.

Independently of the owner fix, bound the per-request fan-out so no single
request can issue an unbounded number of upstream calls: cap the total number of
status-detail requests per report (e.g. a `GitHub:StatusRequestBudget` checked in
the `Parallel.ForEachAsync` body at `PullRequestReportService.cs:63`) and set
`Truncated` when the budget is hit — the report already carries a `Truncated`
flag (`src/GhPrApi/Models/PullRequestReport.cs:11`) for exactly this meaning.

## Resolution
RenderReportAsync rejects any ?owner= that does not case-insensitively match the configured GitHub:Owner, returning 400 'Unsupported owner.' before any GitHub call. Applies to all three routes; both format-suffix routes gained .ProducesProblem(400). Verified against the running container: ?owner=microsoft -> 400, ?owner=ivuorinen -> reaches GitHub. Four new tests cover it, including one asserting the GraphQL client is never called. Deviation from the filed fix: did NOT add a GitHub:StatusRequestBudget option. Constraining the owner already collapses the amplification -- one owner means one cache key means one in-flight fetch through PullRequestReportCoalescer -- and the residual fan-out is bounded by limits the operator sets for their own account. A new option would be speculative config for a bound that already exists. README documents the parameter's new contract.
title: Unauthenticated owner override plus refresh lets any caller exhaust the operator's GitHub token

## Problem

The suite has 53 passing tests across 11 files, all of them unit tests over
normalizers, detectors, formatters, the report builder, the report service, and
the GraphQL client. Not one test exercises an HTTP endpoint. `Program.cs` — which
holds option validation, the rate-limiter policy, format parsing, all six route
handlers, and the exception-to-status-code mapping — has zero coverage.

## Evidence

The test project has no integration-test host:

```text
$ grep -rn "WebApplicationFactory\|Mvc.Testing" tests/
NONE
```

`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/GhPrApi.Tests.csproj:7-18` references only
`Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk`, `xunit`, `xunit.runner.visualstudio`, and
`coverlet.collector` — no `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing`.

Uncovered logic in `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs`:

| Location | Uncovered behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `175-189` | `ParseFormat` — five branches (`null/whitespace`→json, `JSON`, `MARKDOWN`/`MD`, `HTML`, unknown→`null`) |
| `145-152` | unknown `?format=` → 400 Problem Details |
| `117-134` | `GetReadiness` — token-missing 503, unhealthy 503, ready 200 |
| `204-209` | format → content-type mapping (`text/markdown`, `text/html`, JSON) |
| `211-219` | `GitHubQueryException` → 503 in each of the three formats |
| `62-71` | rate-limiter policy: 10/minute, `QueueLimit = 0`, 429 rejection |
| `17-25` | five `Validate` clauses + `ValidateOnStart` |
| `99-113` | the `.json` and `.html` format-fixed route variants |

`README.md` makes precise, testable promises about every one of these — the
exact Markdown error string (`README.md:152-156`), the exact 503 title
(`README.md:136`), the 429 behaviour (`README.md:81`) — and nothing verifies
them.

### Failing scenario

Change `ParseFormat`'s `"MARKDOWN" or "MD"` case to `"MARKDOWN"` only. The full
suite still passes (53/53) while `?format=md`, documented at `README.md:72`,
starts returning 400. The same holds for swapping the `text/markdown` and
`text/html` content types, or dropping `.RequireRateLimiting(...)` from any of
the three routes.

## Impact

Every behaviour a consumer of this API actually depends on — status codes,
content types, error bodies, rate limiting, the format aliases — can regress
without a single test failing. The unit tests cover the parts that compute the
report; nothing covers the parts that serve it.

## Fix

Add `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing` to
`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/GhPrApi.Tests.csproj`:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing" Version="10.0.10" />
```

`Program.cs` uses top-level statements, so expose the generated entry point to
the test project by adding to `src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj`:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <InternalsVisibleTo Include="GhPrApi.Tests" />
</ItemGroup>
```

Then add one `EndpointTests.cs` driving `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` with the
`IGitHubGraphQlClient` replaced by the existing fake pattern from
`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/PullRequestReportServiceTests.cs:119-139`, asserting:

- `?format=` ∈ {absent, `json`, `markdown`, `md`, `html`} → 200 with the
  documented content type; anything else → 400.
- `/api/github/open-pull-requests.json` and `.html` ignore `?format=`.
- A throwing `IGitHubGraphQlClient` → 503 with body exactly
  `Unable to query GitHub.` for markdown, the HTML error page for html, and
  Problem Details with that title for json.
- `/health/ready` → 503 with no token configured, 200 with one.
- The eleventh request inside one minute → 429.

Keep it to a single file; the existing fakes and `TestSupport` cover the setup.

## Resolution
Added Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing to the test project and InternalsVisibleTo(GhPrApi.Tests) to GhPrApi.csproj so WebApplicationFactory<Program> can host the app. New tests/GhPrApi.Tests/EndpointTests.cs adds 24 tests covering every gap the finding listed: all five format aliases and their content types, unknown format -> 400, format-suffix routes ignoring ?format=, owner validation on all three routes, the exact documented 503 body in each of the three formats, readiness with and without a token, the 11th-request 429, and health endpoints being exempt from the limiter. Suite is 77 passing, up from 53. Each test builds its own host so the process-global rate limiter starts with a full window.

## Problem

The service emits no log line for any HTTP request. ASP.NET Core's request
logging lives under the `Microsoft.AspNetCore` category, which
`appsettings.json` raises to `Warning` — successful and client-error requests
are logged at `Information`, so all of them are suppressed. The only logging
anywhere in the application is two warnings on the GitHub failure path.

The success path is entirely dark: who called, with which `?owner=`, whether
`refresh=true` was set, whether the response came from cache or from a full
GitHub scan, and whether the rate limiter rejected anyone.

## Evidence

`src/GhPrApi/appsettings.json:10-15`

```json
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"
    }
  }
```

Every logging call site in `src/`:

```text
$ grep -rn "_logger\.\|UseHttpLogging\|LogInformation" --include=*.cs src/
src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:285:            _logger.LogWarning(
src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:306:            _logger.LogWarning("GitHub GraphQL returned {ErrorCount} errors. ...
```

Two lines, both on the GitHub-failure path. `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs` injects no
`ILogger` and calls no logging middleware. There are no metrics or traces either:

```text
$ grep -rn "OpenTelemetry\|Meter\|ActivitySource\|AddMetrics" --include=*.cs --include=*.csproj src/
NONE
```

### Failing scenario

This compounds the unauthenticated-owner-override finding directly. An operator
notices `503 Unable to query GitHub.` on their own dashboard and investigates:

- The GitHub token's quota is exhausted. The service logs nothing about it —
  `GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:285` fires only once the resilience budget is spent,
  and records the status code and a truncated body, not the owner queried.
- Which `?owner=` values were requested: not logged.
- How many `refresh=true` requests arrived and from where: not logged.
- Whether the rate limiter rejected anything: not logged — `RejectionStatusCode`
  is set (`Program.cs:64`) but 429s are produced by middleware whose category is
  suppressed.

The operator has no way to distinguish "someone is draining my token through
`?owner=`" from "GitHub is having an incident", and no way to identify the
caller in either case.

## Impact

Any incident involving this service is diagnosed without evidence. Abuse of the
public, unauthenticated endpoint is undetectable and unattributable after the
fact. Ordinary questions — request volume, cache hit rate, p99 latency, 429
rate — have no answer.

## Fix

Two changes, both using what is already present.

1. Stop suppressing request logs. `src/GhPrApi/appsettings.json:13`:

```json
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Information"
```

That alone restores a per-request line with method, path, status code, and
duration.

2. Log the two fields that matter for this service's failure mode. In
`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs`, inject
`ILogger<PullRequestReportService>` (the pattern is already established in
`GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:123`) and log one line per upstream fetch in
`FetchAndCacheAsync`:

```csharp
_logger.LogInformation(
    "Fetching open pull requests for {Owner}: {PullRequestCount} PRs, truncated={Truncated}",
    owner, result.PullRequests.Count, result.Truncated);
```

Structured, low cardinality once `owner` is constrained per the owner-override
finding, and it makes cache-miss volume visible — the only number that predicts
GitHub quota consumption.

Do not log tokens or full response bodies. `GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:288` already
truncates the error body to 500 characters via `MaxLoggedErrorBodyLength`; keep
that.

Metrics and tracing are out of scope for a service this size — a request log is
the missing floor, not an observability stack.

## Resolution
appsettings.json keeps Microsoft.AspNetCore at Warning but adds Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.Diagnostics at Information; PullRequestReportService now logs one structured line per upstream fetch with owner, PR count and truncated. Deviation from the filed fix: the finding proposed raising the whole Microsoft.AspNetCore namespace to Information. Measured that against the running container -- it produced six log lines per request (Request starting, Executing endpoint, Setting status code, Writing value, Executed endpoint, Request finished). Narrowing to the one category yields exactly the two lines that matter. Verified in the container: 'Request finished HTTP/1.1 GET .../api/github/open-pull-requests?owner=microsoft&refresh=true - 400 - application/problem+json 77.5308ms' -- the caller, the owner requested, the refresh flag and the outcome are all now visible, which is what the token-drain scenario needed.
title: No request logging: abuse of the public endpoint leaves no trace

## Problem

`README.md:81` documents the rate limit in terms that read as per-caller. The
limiter is a single unpartitioned instance shared by every client of the
process, so one caller's traffic consumes the entire budget for everyone.

## Evidence

`README.md:81`

```text
The endpoint is rate-limited (10 requests/minute per fixed window); a caller over
the limit gets `429 Too Many Requests`. This mainly protects `refresh=true`,
which bypasses the cache and re-queries GitHub in full.
```

"a caller over the limit" implies per-caller accounting. The implementation has
none — `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:65-70`:

```csharp
options.AddFixedWindowLimiter(RateLimiterPolicies.GitHubApi, limiterOptions =>
{
    limiterOptions.PermitLimit = 10;
    limiterOptions.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
    limiterOptions.QueueLimit = 0;
});
```

`AddFixedWindowLimiter(policyName, configureOptions)` builds one
`FixedWindowRateLimiter` for the policy. Per-client accounting requires
`AddPolicy` with a `PartitionedRateLimiter` keyed on the client — there is no
partition key anywhere in the file.

### Failing scenario

An uptime monitor polling `/api/github/open-pull-requests` every 6 seconds
consumes all 10 permits each minute. Every other caller, including the operator,
receives 429 continuously. Read against `README.md:81` an operator would expect
the monitor to be limited to its own 10 and everyone else to be unaffected.

## Impact

Documentation only — the code behaves as designed, and a global cap is the
correct choice for protecting a single shared upstream token. But an operator
sizing `PermitLimit` from this sentence will size it per-client and set it far
too low for the aggregate, or will not realise a single noisy client can starve
the endpoint.

## Fix

Replace `README.md:81` with:

```text
The endpoint is rate-limited to 10 requests per minute (fixed window). The limit
is process-global and shared by all callers, not per client — it exists to cap
total load on the single upstream GitHub token, so one busy caller can exhaust
the window for everyone. A caller over the limit gets `429 Too Many Requests`.
This mainly protects `refresh=true`, which bypasses the cache and re-queries
GitHub in full.
```

## Resolution
README.md rate-limit paragraph rewritten to state the limit is process-global and shared by all callers, not per client, and why (capping total load on the single upstream token). The ?owner= row in the query-parameter table also now documents the value must match the configured owner.
title: README describes the rate limit without saying it is process-global, not per-caller

## Problem

Neither project uses a lockfile, and neither `dotnet restore` invocation runs in
locked mode. CI restores at merge time; the Docker build restores again at image
build time. Nothing guarantees the two resolve the same transitive graph, and
nothing would report it if they diverged.

## Evidence

```text
$ ls src/GhPrApi/packages.lock.json tests/GhPrApi.Tests/packages.lock.json
ls: cannot access 'src/GhPrApi/packages.lock.json': No such file or directory
ls: cannot access 'tests/GhPrApi.Tests/packages.lock.json': No such file or directory
```

`Directory.Build.props:2-9` sets `TreatWarningsAsErrors`, `Nullable`,
`AnalysisLevel`, and `EnforceCodeStyleInBuild` but not
`RestorePackagesWithLockFile`.

Two independent restores of the same commit:

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:25` — `dotnet restore`
- `Dockerfile:10` — `RUN dotnet restore src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj`

Neither passes `--locked-mode`.

That transitive resolution matters here is already established in the repo —
`src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj:11-13`:

```xml
<!-- Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi 10.0.0 transitively pulls Microsoft.OpenApi 2.0.0, which is
     vulnerable to GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc (stack overflow on circular schema refs); pin the fix. -->
<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.OpenApi" Version="2.7.5" />
```

A vulnerable transitive package reached this project once and had to be pinned
by hand. There is no mechanism that would surface the next one at build time.

### Failing scenario

NuGet's `Version="10.0.10"` is a minimum, not a pin — resolution picks the lowest
listed version satisfying each constraint. That is stable while the feed is
stable, so drift is not routine; it occurs when a package version is unlisted or
a direct dependency's own floor moves. When it does, the image built from commit
`X` contains a different dependency graph than the one CI tested for commit `X`,
with no commit, no diff, and no failing check to mark it.

## Impact

Low and latent, not routine. The realistic loss is not nondeterminism but the
absent tripwire: an unexpected transitive change — including a newly introduced
vulnerable package, the exact class of problem already hit once here — enters the
published image silently.

## Fix

Enable lockfiles for both projects in `Directory.Build.props`:

```xml
<RestorePackagesWithLockFile>true</RestorePackagesWithLockFile>
```

Run `dotnet restore` once and commit the generated `packages.lock.json` files
(they must be tracked — `.gitignore` does not currently exclude them).

Then enforce them where restore happens:

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:25`

```yaml
      - name: Restore
        run: dotnet restore --locked-mode
```

`Dockerfile:10`

```dockerfile
RUN dotnet restore src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj --locked-mode
```

With that, any transitive change fails the build until someone regenerates and
reviews the lockfile diff. Dependabot's `nuget` ecosystem
(`.github/dependabot.yml:13-16`) updates lockfiles alongside manifests, so the
existing update flow keeps working.

## Resolution
Directory.Build.props sets RestorePackagesWithLockFile; packages.lock.json generated and present for both projects (confirmed not gitignored). CI restore and the Dockerfile restore both use --locked-mode, and the Dockerfile copies the lockfile before restoring. Verified: 'dotnet restore --locked-mode' succeeds from a clean obj/, and the Docker build completes. Note the XML comment could not contain a literal double-dash, so it describes locked mode in prose.
title: No NuGet lockfile: the image's restore is never the restore CI validated

## Problem

The CI test step collects coverage into `TestResults/`, and the job ends. The
artifact is not uploaded, not published, not compared against a threshold, and
not visible anywhere after the runner is torn down. The flag costs build time
and produces a signal nobody can see.

## Evidence

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:30-31` — the last step in the only job:

```yaml
      - name: Test
        run: dotnet test --configuration Release --no-build --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"
```

There is no `actions/upload-artifact`, no coverage reporter, and no threshold
step anywhere in `.github/workflows/` (the directory holds exactly `ci.yml` and
`container.yml`). `coverlet.collector` is referenced at
`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/GhPrApi.Tests.csproj:14` solely to service this flag.

`.gitignore:7-8` excludes `TestResults/` and `coverage/`, confirming the output
is treated as throwaway.

### Failing scenario

Coverage of `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs` is currently 0% (see the endpoint-test
finding). CI is green. Coverage could fall to 0% across the whole project and CI
would stay green — the collected numbers gate nothing and are discarded when the
runner exits.

## Impact

A non-gating check that reads as a gating one. Anyone looking at the workflow
concludes coverage is tracked; it is not. Minor wasted runner time.

## Fix

Pick one — either make the signal reachable or drop the flag.

Make it visible, in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
      - name: Test
        run: dotnet test --configuration Release --no-build --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage" --results-directory ./TestResults

      - name: Upload coverage
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02 # v4
        with:
          name: coverage
          path: TestResults/**/coverage.cobertura.xml
```

Or drop it, in `.github/workflows/ci.yml:31`:

```yaml
        run: dotnet test --configuration Release --no-build
```

and remove the now-unused `coverlet.collector` reference from
`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/GhPrApi.Tests.csproj:14-17`.

Pin any new action to a commit SHA — every action in both workflows is already
SHA-pinned, and that convention must hold.

## Resolution
ci.yml routes coverage to ./TestResults and uploads it as an artifact via actions/upload-artifact pinned to SHA ea165f8d65b6e75b540449e92b4886f43607fa02, with if-no-files-found: error so a silently missing report fails the step rather than passing quietly. Kept the collector rather than dropping it, since the signal is now reachable. checkov github_actions still passes 60/60.
title: CI collects code coverage that nothing reads or gates on

## Problem

All three Dependabot ecosystems are configured with a schedule and nothing else.
With no `cooldown`, Dependabot opens an update PR as soon as a version is
published — including a version published minutes ago by a compromised
maintainer account, and before the ecosystem has had a chance to yank it.

## Evidence

`.github/dependabot.yml` (entire file):

```yaml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"

  - package-ecosystem: "docker"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"

  - package-ecosystem: "nuget"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
```

Flagged by semgrep `--config=auto`, rule
`package_managers.dependabot.dependabot-missing-cooldown`, severity Blocking,
against all three `package-ecosystem` entries (lines 3-6, 8-11, 13-16):

```text
This Dependabot configuration does not set a cooldown period. Newly published
packages can be malicious or unstable. Add a `cooldown` block with
`default-days: 7` to each `package-ecosystem` entry under `updates` to wait 7
days before proposing updates to newly published package versions.
```

This was the only semgrep finding across the repository; the C# source is clean.

### Failing scenario

A `docker/*-action` or NuGet package is compromised and a malicious patch
version is published on a Monday. Dependabot's weekly run opens a PR against
this repository within days, while the compromise is still undetected. The PR
looks routine — the four most recent commits on `main` are exactly this shape
(`7047b17`, `29d9836`, `e1acddc`, `3a166e7`, all `Bump X from A to B`) — and a
reviewer approving on autopilot merges it. A cooldown window is what buys the
ecosystem time to yank the release before the PR is ever opened.

Nothing auto-merges here, so a human is always in the loop; that is what keeps
this Low rather than higher.

## Impact

The repository takes new dependency versions at their most dangerous moment,
with no delay for the ecosystem to detect and pull a bad release. The existing
mitigations — SHA-pinned actions in both workflows, digest-pinned base images in
the Dockerfile — protect against a tag *moving*, not against a reviewer merging
a Dependabot PR that repoints the pin at a malicious release.

## Fix

Add a cooldown to each ecosystem in `.github/dependabot.yml`:

```yaml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7

  - package-ecosystem: "docker"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7

  - package-ecosystem: "nuget"
    directory: "/"
    schedule:
      interval: "weekly"
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
```

Cooldown does not apply to security updates, so a Dependabot security advisory
still opens a PR immediately — the delay affects routine version bumps only.

While editing the file, consider aligning Dependabot's commit subjects with the
convention the human commits already follow (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:` on
`f658d66`, `1a216e4`, `831c660`, `5a9258a`) by adding to each entry:

```yaml
    commit-message:
      prefix: "chore"
```

That is a consistency nicety, not part of this finding — no release automation
depends on the commit format today.

## Resolution
dependabot.yml adds cooldown.default-days: 7 to all three ecosystems, with a comment noting security advisories are exempt and still open immediately. Also added commit-message.prefix: chore to align Dependabot subjects with the conventional-commit style the human commits already use -- flagged in the finding as an adjacent nicety, applied here since the file was being edited. semgrep --config=auto is now clean across the repository.
title: Dependabot has no cooldown: freshly published versions are proposed immediately

## Problem

`SqliteDistributedCache` documents an absolute fail-open contract: "Every operation fails open:
a `SqliteException` is logged and swallowed, so a read degrades to a miss and a write to a
no-op." But the three runtime methods catch **only** `SqliteException`, while the construction
guard in `Program.cs` catches a strictly wider set — `SqliteException or IOException or
UnauthorizedAccessException`.

The constructor does exactly what `Get`/`Set`/`Remove` do: `OpenConnection()` followed by a
command execution. If those three exception types are reachable from that sequence at startup
(and `Program.cs` asserts they are, by catching them), they are reachable from the identical
sequence at runtime. At runtime nothing catches two of the three.

## Evidence

Startup guard — `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:69`:

```csharp
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is SqliteException or IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException)
```

Runtime guards — `src/GhPrApi/Caching/SqliteDistributedCache.cs:78`, `:116`, `:135`, all three:

```csharp
catch (SqliteException ex)
```

Constructor body (`:50-61`) and `OpenConnection` (`:184-189`) share the same
open-then-execute path as every runtime method, so the reachable exception set is the same.

## Impact

Failing scenario: the container's `/data` volume is remounted read-only, or the host filesystem
fills, mid-process. `SqliteConnection.Open()` or `ExecuteNonQuery()` raises `IOException` /
`UnauthorizedAccessException`. Nothing catches it; it propagates out of `IDistributedCache`
into `HybridCache`, which — as this file's own remark states — "surfaces backend exceptions to
the caller by default". The request fails with HTTP 500 even though GitHub is reachable and
the in-memory tier holds the answer.

That is the exact failure mode commit b6a2f3f ("make the durable cache tier actually fail
open") set out to remove; it was fixed for construction and left open for operation.

## Fix

Widen the three runtime catch clauses to the same filter the startup path uses, and update the
class remark to name the set:

```csharp
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is SqliteException or IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException)
```

Keep `ResolveExpiry`'s `ArgumentException` outside the try, as it already is — the existing
test `Set_still_rejects_an_entry_with_no_absolute_expiry_after_a_corrupt_file` pins that.
Add one test per operation asserting an `IOException` from the backend degrades rather than
propagates.

## Resolution
Get/Set/Remove now route through Execute(), whose catch filter matches Program.cs: SqliteException or IOException or UnauthorizedAccessException.
title: Durable cache fails open only for SqliteException, not the IO failures startup already guards against
