## Problem

`/api/github/open-pull-requests?refresh=true` is unauthenticated and bypasses every cache
tier, forcing a complete re-scan of the owner's repositories against the operator's GitHub
token. The only protection is a process-global fixed-window limiter of 10 requests/minute.
README.md:83 states that limit's purpose explicitly: "it exists to cap total load on the
single upstream GitHub token... This mainly protects `refresh=true`."

It does not. Ten *cache-bypassing* requests per minute is 600 per hour, and each one costs
many upstream GraphQL calls, so the permitted rate exceeds GitHub's hourly budget by roughly
an order of magnitude.

## Evidence

Limiter — `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:107-112`:

```csharp
options.AddFixedWindowLimiter(RateLimiterPolicies.GitHubApi, limiterOptions =>
{
    limiterOptions.PermitLimit = 10;
    limiterOptions.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
    limiterOptions.QueueLimit = 0;
});
```

`refresh` reaches the service unauthenticated and disables both read tiers —
`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:45-47`:

```csharp
var flags = refresh
    ? HybridCacheEntryFlags.DisableLocalCacheRead | HybridCacheEntryFlags.DisableDistributedCacheRead
    : HybridCacheEntryFlags.None;
```

The same `flags` value is threaded into the per-PR status cache
(`PullRequestReportService.cs:82` -> `GetStatusDetailsAsync(..., flags, ...)` -> `:142`), so a
refresh re-fetches every PR's status too. `PullRequestReportServiceTests`
`A_settled_status_survives_a_listing_refresh` measures this directly: after one `refresh: true`
call, `StatusCallCount` is 2, not 1 — nothing is reused.

Cost per refresh, with `MaxRepositoryPageSize = 10`
(`src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:21`): `ceil(repos / 10)` listing requests plus one
status request per open PR. For a modest 50 repositories with 40 open PRs that is 5 listing
requests (~10 points each at 10 repos x 100 PRs) plus 40 status requests, roughly 90 points.

At the permitted 600 refreshes/hour: **~54,000 points/hour against GitHub GraphQL's 5,000
points/hour budget.**

## Impact

Failing scenario: an unauthenticated client runs
`while true; do curl -s '.../open-pull-requests?refresh=true'; sleep 6; done`. It stays inside
the rate limit permanently and exhausts the token's hourly GraphQL budget in minutes. GitHub
then rejects every query, `ExecuteAsync` throws `GitHubQueryException`, and **every** caller —
including cached ones once the TTL rolls — gets `503 Unable to query GitHub.` until the hour
resets. One unauthenticated caller takes the service down repeatedly, and the operator's token
is the resource being burned.

The plain read path is not the problem: it is cache-served and cheap. `refresh` is the one
parameter that converts an inbound request into unbounded upstream cost, and it shares the
same permit budget as the cheap path.

## Fix

Give the expensive path its own, much tighter budget instead of letting it share the cheap
path's. In `Program.cs`, replace the single policy with a partitioned limiter keyed on whether
the request asks for a refresh:

```csharp
options.AddPolicy(RateLimiterPolicies.GitHubApi, httpContext =>
{
    var refresh = string.Equals(httpContext.Request.Query["refresh"], "true", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
    return RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter(
        refresh ? "refresh" : "cached",
        _ => new FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions
        {
            // A refresh costs a full upstream re-scan; one per minute still beats the 300s
            // listing TTL, and stays two orders of magnitude inside GitHub's hourly budget.
            PermitLimit = refresh ? 1 : 10,
            Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1),
            QueueLimit = 0,
        });
});
```

Then correct README.md:83 to state the two separate limits. Add an endpoint test asserting the
second `?refresh=true` inside one window returns 429 while a plain read still returns 200.

## Resolution
Rate limiter partitioned on refresh: 1/min for cache-bypassing calls, 10/min for cached reads, independent budgets. Covered by Refresh_has_its_own_far_tighter_budget_than_a_cached_read.
title: Unauthenticated ?refresh=true drains the GitHub token quota; the 10/min limit is an order of magnitude too loose to stop it

## Problem

`CiNormalizer.Normalize` returns `passing` whenever the set of *required* checks is empty and
branch protection does not require status checks — regardless of what the non-required checks
actually reported. In a repository without branch protection, every check is non-required, so
a pull request whose entire CI run is red is reported as `"ci": "passing"`.

This was already a wrong field value. The uncommitted "Easy wins" feature promotes it into a
wrong recommendation: `IsEasyWin` tests `Ci == passing`, so those PRs are now listed in a
section README.md:247 describes as "the PRs that can be merged right now".

## Evidence

`src/GhPrApi/Services/CiNormalizer.cs:55-61`:

```csharp
var requiredChecks = SelectRequiredChecks(statusDetails).ToArray();
if (requiredChecks.Length == 0)
{
    return statusDetails.RequiresStatusChecks
        ? NormalizedValues.Ci.Pending
        : NormalizedValues.Ci.Passing;
}
```

`SelectRequiredChecks` (`:78-84`) with no `RequiredStatusCheckNames` falls back to
`StatusChecks.Where(check => check.IsRequired)`. `IsRequired` is GitHub's
`isRequired(pullRequestNumber:)` field, which is `false` for every check when no branch
protection rule requires it (`GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:102`, `:107`). `RequiresStatusChecks` is
`branchProtectionRule?.RequiresStatusChecks == true` (`GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:268`), i.e.
`false` when there is no rule at all.

So: unprotected repository -> `requiredChecks` empty -> `RequiresStatusChecks` false ->
`passing`, with the failing `CheckRun` nodes present in `StatusChecks` and simply not consulted.

Consumed by the new feature — `src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportBuilder.cs:209-213`:

```csharp
private static bool IsEasyWin(PullRequestItem item) =>
    !item.IsDraft
    && item.Ci.Equals(NormalizedValues.Ci.Passing, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)
    ...
```

README.md's CI table (`:229-234`) documents four rules — failing, pending, "all required checks
successful -> passing", "unclear -> pending". None of them covers "no required checks at all",
and the observed behaviour matches neither the third (nothing succeeded) nor the fourth
(it returns passing, not pending).

## Impact

Failing scenario: `ivuorinen/example` has a GitHub Actions workflow but no branch protection.
PR #7's build fails. The report shows `"ci": "passing"` and lists #7 under **Easy wins** as
ready to merge. Acting on that section — its entire purpose — merges a PR with a red build.

This is not a rare corner: branch protection is off by default on new repositories, and this
service scans *every* public repository of an owner, so the unprotected ones are exactly the
long tail it is most useful for.

## Fix

When nothing is required but checks did run, fall back to the checks that exist rather than
declaring victory:

```csharp
var requiredChecks = SelectRequiredChecks(statusDetails).ToArray();
if (requiredChecks.Length == 0)
{
    if (statusDetails.RequiresStatusChecks)
    {
        return NormalizedValues.Ci.Pending;
    }

    // No branch protection: nothing is required, so nothing blocks a merge -- but reporting
    // "passing" while red checks sit in StatusChecks is a lie the Easy wins section acts on.
    // Judge the checks that actually ran; only a repository with no checks at all is passing.
    return statusDetails.StatusChecks.Count == 0
        ? NormalizedValues.Ci.Passing
        : NormalizeAgainst(statusDetails.StatusChecks);
}
```

where `NormalizeAgainst` is the existing failing/pending/passing cascade at `:63-75` extracted
into a method taking the check list. Add tests: red non-required check -> `failing`; no checks
at all -> `passing`; and a builder test asserting the red-but-unprotected PR is absent from
Easy wins. Then add the "no required checks" row to README.md's CI table.

## Resolution
CiNormalizer now judges the checks that ran when nothing is required; only a repo with zero checks reads passing. Three CiNormalizer tests plus Easy_wins_excludes_a_red_pull_request_in_an_unprotected_repository. README CI rules updated.
title: A repository with no branch protection reports ci: passing even when its checks are red, and now lands in Easy wins

## Problem

GitHub's GraphQL API returns `data: { "repositoryOwner": null }` with **no `errors` array**
when the `login` does not resolve to a user or organization. `GetOpenPullRequestsAsync` treats
that null as "this page had no repositories" and returns an empty, successful result.

A typo in `GitHub:Owner`, or an account that was renamed or deleted, therefore produces a
permanently green, permanently empty service: it starts, passes `/health/ready`, reports
`gitHubReachable: true`, and serves `{"totalCount": 0, "message": "No open PRs."}` forever.
That is byte-identical to the legitimate "the owner genuinely has no open PRs" response, so
there is nothing for an operator to notice.

## Evidence

`src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:172-176`:

```csharp
var repositories = response.RepositoryOwner?.Repositories;
if (repositories is null)
{
    return new GitHubOpenPullRequestsResult(pullRequests, truncated);
}
```

`RepositoryOwner` is nullable by declaration (`:377`):

```csharp
private sealed record OpenPullRequestsData(RepositoryOwnerNode? RepositoryOwner);
```

The `errors`-array path at `:306-312` never fires for an unknown login — GitHub answers a
nullable field with `null` and HTTP 200, not an error. `ExecuteAsync` then calls
`_healthState.RecordSuccess()` at `:320`, so readiness reports GitHub as reachable, which it
is; the owner simply is not.

No test covers this: `GitHubGraphQlClientTests` has cases for HTTP failure (`:164`), a GraphQL
`errors` array (`:179`), single-page and multi-page success, but none for
`repositoryOwner: null`.

## Impact

Failing scenario: an operator deploys with `GitHub__Owner=ivuorinnen` (one transposed letter,
or an org that was renamed). Startup validation passes — the option is only checked for
non-empty (`Program.cs:35`). `/health/ready` returns `200 {"status":"ready"}`. Every report
request returns `200 {"totalCount":0,"message":"No open PRs."}`. Every dashboard consuming
this reads "no work to do". The misconfiguration is invisible until somebody manually compares
against GitHub.

## Fix

A null owner on the **first** page is a configuration error, not an empty result. Distinguish
the two — on later pages a null owner would mean the account disappeared mid-scan, which is
equally worth surfacing:

```csharp
var repositories = response.RepositoryOwner?.Repositories;
if (repositories is null)
{
    // GitHub answers an unknown login with a null repositoryOwner and no errors array, so this
    // is the only place a misspelled or renamed owner can be detected. Returning empty here
    // would render a misconfiguration indistinguishable from "no open PRs".
    throw new GitHubQueryException($"GitHub owner '{owner}' was not found.");
}
```

The endpoint already maps `GitHubQueryException` to `503 Unable to query GitHub.`
(`Program.cs:271-279`), which is the correct visible outcome. Add a client test feeding
`{"data":{"repositoryOwner":null}}` and asserting `GitHubQueryException`.

## Resolution
A null repositoryOwner now throws GitHubQueryException naming the owner. Covered by GetOpenPullRequestsAsync_throws_when_the_owner_does_not_exist.
title: A misspelled or renamed GitHub:Owner reports 200 with an empty report instead of an error

body: ## Problem `MarkdownReportFormatter` writes GitHub-sourced strings — PR title, author login, dependency group name — straight into the response with no escaping. The HTML formatter escapes the same values through `WebUtility.HtmlEncode` and has a dedicated test proving it; the Markdown formatter has neither, and README.md documents the guarantee only for HTML. PR titles on public repositories are attacker-controlled: any outside contributor can open a PR with an arbitrary title, and this service scans *every* public repository of the configured owner, so those titles land in the response without the operator ever touching them. ## Evidence Unescaped — `src/GhPrApi/Services/MarkdownReportFormatter.cs:82-97`: ```csharp builder .Append(pullRequest.Id) .Append(": ") .Append(pullRequest.Title) .Append(" — ") .Append(pullRequest.Author) ``` Escaped, by contrast — `src/GhPrApi/Services/HtmlReportFormatter.cs:113`, `:125`: ```csharp .Append("").Append(Encode(pullRequest.Title)).Append(""); ... private static string Encode(string value) => WebUtility.HtmlEncode(value); ``` Test asymmetry: `HtmlReportFormatterTests.Format_html_encodes_untrusted_github_content` (`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/HtmlReportFormatterTests.cs:81-98`) feeds `""` and asserts it does not survive. `MarkdownReportFormatterTests` has no counterpart — no test in the suite passes hostile input through the Markdown path. Documentation asymmetry: README.md:197 promises "All GitHub-sourced text (titles, authors) is HTML-encoded" for the HTML response. The Markdown section (`:170-193`) makes no claim either way, so a consumer has no stated contract to rely on. ## Impact Failing scenario: an outside contributor opens a PR on a public repo of the configured owner titled ``. `?format=markdown` returns it verbatim. Any consumer that renders this Markdown with raw HTML enabled — the common default in dashboards, static-site pipelines, and most JS Markdown renderers — executes it in that consumer's origin. The XSS the HTML path deliberately blocks is served unblocked one query parameter away. Secondary, non-security: a title containing `[`, `]`, `` ` `` or a leading `#` corrupts the list structure the README documents as the stable Markdown shape. ## Fix Escape the characters that can either introduce raw HTML or break the bullet's structure. The rendered text stays readable; only the markup-significant characters change. Add to `MarkdownReportFormatter`: ```csharp // GitHub-sourced text is attacker-controlled: any outside contributor picks the PR title. // Escaping < and the inline-markup characters keeps a hostile title from smuggling raw HTML // into a downstream renderer, or from breaking the documented one-PR-per-bullet shape. private static string Escape(string value) { var escaped = new StringBuilder(value.Length); foreach (var c in value) { if (c is '<' or '>' or '[' or ']' or '`' or '*' or '_' or '\\') { escaped.Append('\\'); } escaped.Append(c is '\r' or '\n' ? ' ' : c); } return escaped.ToString(); } ``` and route `Title`, `Author`, and `dependencyGroup.DependencyName` through it. Add a `Format_escapes_untrusted_github_content` test mirroring the HTML one, and state the guarantee in README.md's Markdown section. ## Resolution Titles and dependency names escaped for < > [ ] backtick backslash, newlines collapsed. Authors deliberately left alone (GitHub restricts logins). Covered by Format_escapes_untrusted_github_content; README documents the guarantee.

## Problem

The repository listing is capped and, when the cap bites, says so via `truncated`. The work
*derived* from that listing — one GraphQL status request per open pull request — has no cap and
no signal at all. One inbound HTTP request expands into as many upstream requests as the owner
has open PRs, bounded only by the product of two limits whose defaults are 1000 and 100.

## Evidence

Fan-out — `src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:70-94`:

```csharp
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    Enumerable.Range(0, listing.PullRequests.Count),
    new ParallelOptions
    {
        MaxDegreeOfParallelism = MaxConcurrentStatusRequests,   // 8
        CancellationToken = cancellationToken,
    },
    async (index, token) => { ... await GetStatusDetailsAsync(...) ... });
```

`MaxConcurrentStatusRequests` (`:13`) throttles *concurrency*, not *total*. Nothing bounds
`listing.PullRequests.Count`.

The permitted ceiling comes from the validated option ranges in `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:37-38`:

```csharp
.Validate(options => options.RepositoryLimit is >= 1 and <= 1_000, ...)
.Validate(options => options.PullRequestLimitPerRepository is >= 1 and <= 100, ...)
```

and the defaults in `src/GhPrApi/Options/GitHubOptions.cs:13-15` sit at the top of both ranges:
`RepositoryLimit = 1_000`, `PullRequestLimitPerRepository = 100`. **100,000 status requests is
the default-configuration ceiling**, not an exotic setting someone has to opt into.

Contrast the listing, which is bounded *and* reports it —
`src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:197-200`:

```csharp
if (hasNextPage)
{
    truncated = true;
}
```

There is no equivalent for the status phase. `truncated` is documented (README.md:145) as
covering `RepositoryLimit` and `PullRequestLimitPerRepository` only.

## Impact

Failing scenario: the service is pointed at an organization with 300 public repositories
averaging 5 open PRs — 1,500 PRs, well inside every configured limit, so `truncated` is
`false`. The first request after a cold start (a redeploy without the `/data` volume, which
README.md:168 explicitly presents as a supported degraded mode) issues 30 listing requests plus
1,500 status requests. At 8-way concurrency and ~300ms per call that is roughly a **60-second
HTTP response**, with no request timeout configured anywhere to cut it short.

GitHub's 5,000-point hourly GraphQL budget runs out partway through. The remaining status
queries throw `GitHubQueryException`, each caught per-PR (`:85-93`), so the request completes
with a `degraded: true` report in which most PRs read `ci: "unknown"` — and `truncated: false`,
because the listing itself was complete. The response says the data is whole; it is not.

At the 1000x100 ceiling this is a request that cannot finish in any useful time.

## Fix

Bound the derived work the same way the listing is bounded, and reuse the existing signal.
In `PullRequestReportService.GetOpenPullRequestsAsync`, before the fan-out:

```csharp
private const int MaxStatusRequestsPerReport = 500;

// The listing is capped and says so via `truncated`; the work derived from it was not. One
// inbound request must not turn into an unbounded number of upstream calls -- at the default
// 1000x100 limits that is 100,000, which exhausts the token's hourly budget and cannot finish.
var statusBudget = Math.Min(listing.PullRequests.Count, MaxStatusRequestsPerReport);
var statusTruncated = statusBudget < listing.PullRequests.Count;
```

Enrich the first `statusBudget` PRs, leave the remainder with `StatusUnresolved = true` (which
already renders as `ci: "unknown"` via `PullRequestReportBuilder.cs:146-148`), and OR
`statusTruncated` into the `truncated` flag passed to `_builder.Build`. Add a
`GitHub:StatusRequestBudget` option so operators can raise it deliberately, and document the
third `truncated` cause in README.md:145.

## Resolution
MaxStatusRequestsPerReport = 500; PRs past the budget report ci: unknown and set truncated (not degraded). Covered by Status_fan_out_is_capped_and_reported_as_truncated; README lists the third truncated cause.
title: The per-PR status fan-out is unbounded: default limits permit 100,000 upstream calls for one inbound request

## Problem

The test named `A_settled_status_survives_a_listing_refresh` asserts
`Assert.Equal(2, gitHub.StatusCallCount)` — i.e. that the settled status was **re-fetched**,
which is the precise negation of "survives". The test passes, so nobody notices; it is pinning
the behaviour its name denies.

## Evidence

`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/PullRequestReportServiceTests.cs:179-194`:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task A_settled_status_survives_a_listing_refresh()
{
    ...
    await service.GetOpenPullRequestsAsync(null, refresh: false, CancellationToken.None);
    await service.GetOpenPullRequestsAsync(null, refresh: true, CancellationToken.None);

    Assert.Equal(2, gitHub.ListingCallCount);
    Assert.Equal(2, gitHub.StatusCallCount);   // <-- fetched twice: it did NOT survive
}
```

One PR is in the listing, so one status call per report. Two status calls means the second
report re-queried it rather than reusing the cached entry.

The behaviour is real and intentional: `refresh` produces
`DisableLocalCacheRead | DisableDistributedCacheRead`
(`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:45-47`) and that same `flags` value is
handed to the per-PR status cache at `:82` and `:142`. So `?refresh=true` bypasses the status
cache too. Only the name is wrong.

Contrast `Retry_after_partial_failure_only_refetches_the_missing_prs` (`:151-177`), which
genuinely tests survival and asserts 4 calls rather than 6 — that one is correct.

## Impact

Failing scenario for a future maintainer: someone reads
`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs`, decides `?refresh=true` should scope to the
listing and leave 6-hour-settled statuses alone (a defensible reading of README.md:166, "a
refresh only re-queries what can actually have changed"), and implements it. The test named
`A_settled_status_survives_a_listing_refresh` now fails. The obvious conclusion — "my change
broke the settled-status-survives guarantee" — is exactly backwards, and the change gets
reverted for the wrong reason.

A test whose name contradicts its assertion is worse than no test: it actively misleads the
next reader about which behaviour is intended.

## Fix

Rename to state what is asserted, and say why in a comment, since the intent is not obvious:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Refresh_bypasses_the_per_pr_status_cache_too()
{
    // ?refresh=true threads DisableLocalCacheRead|DisableDistributedCacheRead into the status
    // cache as well as the listing, so a settled 6h entry is re-fetched. That is deliberate:
    // refresh is the documented escape hatch for a re-run against an unchanged head SHA.
    ...
    Assert.Equal(2, gitHub.ListingCallCount);
    Assert.Equal(2, gitHub.StatusCallCount);
}
```

If survival across refresh is actually wanted, that is a behaviour change and belongs in a
separate decision — but the test must not straddle both readings.

## Resolution
Renamed to Refresh_bypasses_the_per_pr_status_cache_too, with a comment explaining why two status calls is the intended result.
title: A_settled_status_survives_a_listing_refresh asserts the opposite of what its name claims

## Problem

`GitHubGraphQlClientTests` covers `GetOpenPullRequestsAsync` from nine angles — mapping,
pagination, both truncation causes, HTTP failure, GraphQL errors, health-state transitions,
and a node-count ceiling guard. It covers `GetPullRequestStatusDetailsAsync` **zero** times.
No test in the suite deserializes a `PullRequestStatusQuery` response.

That method owns non-trivial parsing logic that feeds every CI verdict in the product, and it
is the only place the two distinct branch-protection shapes GitHub returns get reconciled.

## Evidence

Every test in `tests/GhPrApi.Tests/GitHubGraphQlClientTests.cs` calls
`client.GetOpenPullRequestsAsync(...)` (`:91`, `:106`, `:131`, `:145`, `:157`, `:173`, `:186`,
`:199`) or reflects over a query constant (`:22`, `:113`). `GetPullRequestStatusDetailsAsync`
appears nowhere.

The untested logic in `src/GhPrApi/GitHub/GitHubGraphQlClient.cs:205-269`:

1. **Display-name fallback** (`:229-231`) — `CheckRun` supplies `name`, `StatusContext`
   supplies `context`; the code picks whichever is non-blank and drops the check entirely if
   both are (`:241`).
2. **Two-source required-name merge** (`:245-261`) — `requiredStatusCheckContexts` (a plain
   string list) and `requiredStatusChecks { context }` (an object list) are both read into one
   case-insensitive `HashSet`. GitHub populates these differently depending on whether the rule
   was created through the classic or the newer API, so a repo may deliver one, the other, or
   both with different casing.
3. **`IReadOnlySet` -> array conversion** (`:263-267`), which exists solely because
   `System.Text.Json` cannot round-trip `IReadOnlySet` through the HybridCache L2 — a
   constraint recorded in a comment in `GitHubModels.cs:32-34` and enforced by nothing.

The layer above is well covered — `CiNormalizerTests` exercises `SelectRequiredChecks` against
hand-built `GitHubPullRequestStatusDetails` values. But that starts *after* the parsing under
discussion; nothing checks that real GraphQL JSON produces those values.

## Impact

Failing scenario: GitHub returns a branch protection rule that populates only
`requiredStatusChecks` (objects) and leaves `requiredStatusCheckContexts` null — the shape
rulesets produce. If a refactor drops the second loop at `:255-261`, `requiredNames` comes back
empty, `SelectRequiredChecks` falls through to `Where(check => check.IsRequired)`, and — per
the empty-required path in `CiNormalizer:55-61` — every PR in that repository reports
`ci: passing`. The full suite stays green: no test feeds that JSON.

The same silence covers a regression in the display-name fallback, which would drop every
`StatusContext` check (legacy commit statuses) from consideration.

## Fix

Add three tests to `GitHubGraphQlClientTests`, reusing the existing `FakeHttpMessageHandler`
and `JsonResponse` helpers:

1. `GetPullRequestStatusDetailsAsync_maps_check_runs_and_status_contexts` — a response with one
   `CheckRun` (`name`) and one `StatusContext` (`context`); assert both survive with the right
   `DisplayName`, and that a node with neither is dropped.
2. `GetPullRequestStatusDetailsAsync_merges_both_required_check_sources` — populate
   `requiredStatusCheckContexts: ["Build"]` and `requiredStatusChecks: [{context: "build"}]`;
   assert `RequiredStatusCheckNames` has exactly one entry (the case-insensitive `HashSet`
   dedupe at `:245`).
3. `GetPullRequestStatusDetailsAsync_handles_a_repository_with_no_branch_protection` — `ref`
   null; assert `RequiresStatusChecks` is false and `RequiredStatusCheckNames` is empty.

## Resolution
Added three GetPullRequestStatusDetailsAsync tests: CheckRun/StatusContext name fallback and blank-name drop, both required-source merge with case-insensitive dedupe, and the no-branch-protection shape.
title: GetPullRequestStatusDetailsAsync has no tests at all: the required-check merge and name fallback are unverified

## Problem

The CI workflow restores, builds, tests and uploads coverage. It never checks whether any
restored package carries a known advisory. Nothing in the pipeline fails on a vulnerable
dependency; detection is left entirely to Dependabot, which is asynchronous and does not gate
a merge.

This repository has already been bitten by exactly that gap once.

## Evidence

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the complete step list is Checkout, Setup .NET, Restore, Build,
Test, Upload coverage. No scanning step of any kind.

The prior incident is recorded in the codebase itself. `src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj` carries an
explicit `Microsoft.OpenApi` reference whose comment exists only to dodge an advisory, and
`tests/GhPrApi.Tests/EndpointTests.cs:141-144` names it:

```csharp
// Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi declares only Microsoft.OpenApi >= 2.0.0, so the
// explicit reference that dodges GHSA-v5pm-xwqc-g5wc can drag the runtime across a
// major version.
```

The two `SQLitePCLRaw` pins exist for the same reason — `docs/audit/findings/deps/open/deps-64429a6d.md`
records that "this repository has already been bitten once by a transitive
(GHSA-2m69-gcr7-jv3q), which is why the pins exist at all."

So the project's defence against vulnerable transitives is currently three hand-maintained
version pins with explanatory comments, and no automated check that they are still doing their
job. `dotnet restore --locked-mode` guarantees reproducibility, not safety: it will faithfully
restore a known-vulnerable graph.

Verified locally that the gate would be cheap and currently green:

```text
$ dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive
The given project `GhPrApi` has no vulnerable packages given the current sources.
The given project `GhPrApi.Tests` has no vulnerable packages given the current sources.
```

## Impact

Failing scenario: an advisory is published against a transitive of `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`
or `SQLitePCLRaw`. The lockfile pins the vulnerable version, so every CI run restores it and
passes green. Dependabot opens a PR — but `.github/dependabot.yml` applies `cooldown:
default-days: 7` to the nuget ecosystem, so routine bumps wait a week (security advisories are
exempt, but only once GitHub links the advisory to the package). In the meantime every merge to
main builds and publishes a container image carrying the vulnerable dependency, with nothing
in the pipeline saying so.

## Fix

Add one gating step to `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, after Restore. `dotnet list package
--vulnerable` exits 0 even when it finds something, so the failure has to be asserted on the
output:

```yaml
      # Locked-mode restore guarantees reproducibility, not safety: it will faithfully restore
      # a known-vulnerable graph. This repo has shipped one (GHSA-2m69-gcr7-jv3q); the pins that
      # fixed it need a check that they still hold.
      - name: Check for vulnerable packages
        run: |
          dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive 2>&1 | tee vulnerable.txt
          ! grep -q 'has the following vulnerable packages' vulnerable.txt
```

Place it before Build so a vulnerable graph fails fast. `--include-transitive` is the point:
both historical incidents were transitives.

## Resolution
CI gained a 'Check for vulnerable packages' step running dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive and asserting on the output, since the command exits 0 regardless.
title: CI has no dependency-vulnerability gate, in a repo that already shipped a vulnerable transitive once

## Problem

`CI` and `Container` are two independent workflows triggered by the same event. Neither waits
for the other. On every push to `main` they start simultaneously, and `Container` pushes
`latest` to GHCR without ever learning whether `Build and test` passed.

The publish is not gated on anything.

## Evidence

Both fire on the same trigger.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
```

`.github/workflows/container.yml`:

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
    tags:
      - 'v*.*.*'
  workflow_dispatch:
```

`container.yml` has exactly one job, `publish`, whose steps are Checkout, Buildx, Login,
Metadata, Build-and-push. There is no `needs:`, no `workflow_run:` trigger, and no test step of
its own. `docker/build-push-action` runs with `push: true` unconditionally.

The tags it publishes include the moving one — `container.yml` metadata step:

```yaml
          tags: |
            type=ref,event=branch
            type=ref,event=tag
            type=sha,prefix=sha-
            type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}}
```

`type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}}` means every push to `main` moves `latest`.

The tag trigger is worse: `tags: ['v*.*.*']` fires on a pushed release tag, and a tag push does
not run `ci.yml` at all (`ci.yml` restricts its push trigger to `branches: [main]`). A tagged
release image is therefore published with **no** CI run associated with it whatsoever.

## Impact

Failing scenario: a commit lands on `main` that compiles but breaks a test — a merge of two
individually-green PRs that conflict semantically is the classic case, and it is exactly the
case a PR check cannot catch, since neither PR was tested against the other's merged state.

`CI` starts and will go red in ~90 seconds. `Container` starts at the same moment and, being a
Docker build with GHA cache, often finishes first. `ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:latest` now
points at the broken commit. README.md:360 tells Coolify to deploy exactly that tag:

> | Image | `ghcr.io/ivuorinen/gh-pr-api:latest` |

so the broken build is now the deployable artifact, and the red CI run that would have said so
arrives after the fact. Nothing rolls it back.

## Fix

Gate the publish on the test workflow instead of the push. Replace the trigger in
`.github/workflows/container.yml`:

```yaml
on:
  # workflow_run, not push: CI and Container both fired on push and raced, so `latest` could be
  # published from a commit whose tests were still running -- or already red.
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["CI"]
    types: [completed]
    branches: [main]
  push:
    tags:
      - 'v*.*.*'
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  publish:
    # A workflow_run fires on failure too; only a green CI may publish. Tag and manual runs have
    # no CI run to inspect and are gated by who can push a tag.
    if: github.event_name != 'workflow_run' || github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'
```

`workflow_run` checks out the default branch by default, so pin the ref explicitly in the
checkout step:

```yaml
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_run' && github.event.workflow_run.head_sha || github.ref }}
          persist-credentials: false
```

For the tag path, extend `ci.yml`'s push trigger to include `tags: ['v*.*.*']` so a release tag
is tested at all.

## Resolution
Fixed differently than filed: the workflow_run approach zizmor flags as a dangerous trigger (a fork can name its branch main), so container.yml was merged into ci.yml as a publish job with needs: build-test and a non-PR/default-branch-or-tag guard. Per-job concurrency preserves both cancel semantics. actionlint and zizmor clean.
title: The container workflow publishes latest in parallel with CI, so an image can ship from a commit whose tests fail

## Problem

`compose.yml` consumes eight `GITHUB_*` variables. `.env.example` documents six of them.
`GITHUB_CACHE_PATH` and `GITHUB_STATUS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS` are missing — the two newest, both
added by the cache-split work — and README.md points at the file as authoritative.

## Evidence

`compose.yml` reads both:

```yaml
      GitHub__CachePath: "${GITHUB_CACHE_PATH:-/data/cache.db}"
      GitHub__StatusCacheTtlSeconds: "${GITHUB_STATUS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS:-30}"
```

`.env.example` in full:

```text
GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_or_ghp_token
GITHUB_OWNER=ivuorinen
GITHUB_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=300
GITHUB_REPOSITORY_LIMIT=1000
GITHUB_PR_LIMIT_PER_REPO=100
GITHUB_STATUS_CHECK_LIMIT=100
IMAGE_TAG=latest
```

README.md:321-323 makes the claim the file no longer satisfies:

> Every setting in `compose.yml` is overridable from `.env` — see `.env.example` for the full
> list (`GITHUB_OWNER`, `GITHUB_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS`, `IMAGE_TAG`, …). Defaults match the in-code
> defaults, so an empty `.env` beyond `GITHUB_TOKEN` behaves exactly as documented.

The second sentence is also inaccurate for `GITHUB_CACHE_PATH`: compose defaults it to
`/data/cache.db`, whereas the in-code default is `cache.db` (`src/GhPrApi/Options/GitHubOptions.cs:19`).
The compose default is the correct one for a container — it just is not the in-code default,
and the README says it is.

## Impact

Failing scenario: an operator following README.md's "Create `.env` from `.env.example`" flow
wants the durable cache on a bind mount rather than the named volume, or wants a longer status
TTL to cut GitHub calls. They read `.env.example`, which README calls the full list, conclude
neither knob is exposed, and edit `compose.yml` directly — putting a deployment-specific value
into a tracked file, which is exactly what the `.env` indirection exists to prevent.

The `StatusCacheTtlSeconds` case is the more costly one: it is the main lever on upstream
GitHub quota consumption, and it is the one the file hides.

## Fix

Append both to `.env.example`, matching the compose defaults:

```text
# Durable cache tier. Must sit on the mounted volume to survive a redeploy.
GITHUB_CACHE_PATH=/data/cache.db
# TTL for a PR whose checks are still running. Failing checks use twice this; an all-green
# verdict is cached for 6 hours, keyed by head commit SHA.
GITHUB_STATUS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS=30
```

and correct README.md:322-323 to drop "Defaults match the in-code defaults" in favour of naming
the one place they deliberately differ:

> Defaults match the in-code defaults, except `GITHUB_CACHE_PATH`, which points at the mounted
> volume (`/data/cache.db`) rather than the code's relative `cache.db`.

## Resolution
Wrong: .env.example already declares GITHUB_CACHE_PATH and GITHUB_STATUS_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS with explanatory comments. The finding was written from a chunk-truncated read of the file. The one real sub-point -- README claiming compose defaults match the in-code defaults, which is untrue for CachePath -- was corrected in README.md.
title: .env.example omits two variables compose.yml reads, while README calls it the full list

## Problem

README.md's query-parameter table describes `refresh` as affecting one cache tier. It affects
three things: the in-memory tier, the SQLite durable tier, and the per-PR status cache — the
last of which the README elsewhere presents as the mechanism that makes refreshes cheap.

## Evidence

README.md:73:

> | `refresh` | no | If `true`, bypasses the current in-memory cache. |

What the code does — `src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:45-47`:

```csharp
var flags = refresh
    ? HybridCacheEntryFlags.DisableLocalCacheRead | HybridCacheEntryFlags.DisableDistributedCacheRead
    : HybridCacheEntryFlags.None;
```

`DisableDistributedCacheRead` is the SQLite tier — the second one the README documents at
`:168`. The same `flags` value is then passed to the per-PR status cache (`:82`, `:142`), so
every settled status is re-fetched too.

`PullRequestReportServiceTests` measures exactly that: after one `refresh: true` call,
`StatusCallCount` is 2 for a single-PR listing, not 1.

This matters against README.md:166, which sells the split as:

> The consequence is that a refresh only re-queries what can actually have changed, and a
> failure part-way through keeps everything that already succeeded.

That describes SHA-keyed invalidation on the normal path. It reads, in a section titled
Caching, as a statement about `?refresh=`, which is the one path where it is false — an
explicit refresh re-queries everything, changed or not.

## Impact

Failing scenario: an operator watching a slow CI run polls `?refresh=true` every few seconds,
reading the table as "skips the 300s in-memory listing TTL, keeps the cheap parts". Each call
instead re-fetches the listing *and* one status query per open PR against the shared token
budget — see the quota finding on `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs`. The documentation is what makes
the expensive call look cheap.

## Fix

Correct the table row:

> | `refresh` | no | If `true`, bypasses **both** cache tiers and the per-PR status cache, re-querying GitHub in full. Costs one listing request per 10 repositories plus one request per open PR. |

and disambiguate `:166` by scoping the sentence to the normal path:

> The consequence is that an ordinary request only re-queries what can actually have changed,
> and a failure part-way through keeps everything that already succeeded. `?refresh=true` is
> the deliberate exception: it re-queries everything, which is what makes it the escape hatch
> for a CI re-run against an unchanged head commit.

## Resolution
README's refresh row now states it bypasses both tiers and the per-PR status cache, with its upstream cost; the caching section scopes its cheap-refresh claim to the ordinary path.
title: README describes ?refresh= as bypassing 'the in-memory cache'; it bypasses both tiers and the per-PR status cache

## Problem

The HTML report wraps each table in `div.table-wrap` with `overflow-x: auto`. A scrollable
region is an interactive control, and this one has no way to receive keyboard focus. A keyboard
or switch user cannot scroll it; they can only reach content that happens to sit under a
focusable element.

## Evidence

`src/GhPrApi/Services/HtmlReportFormatter.cs:15`:

```css
.table-wrap { overflow-x: auto; margin-top: 0.5rem; }
```

`:100` emits it with no `tabindex` and no accessible name:

```csharp
builder.Append("<div class=\"table-wrap\">\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>");
```

The table's only focusable content is the PR-title link in column 2 of seven
(`:113`). Tabbing to a link scrolls it into view, so columns 1-2 are reachable. Columns 3-7 —
Author, Age, Review, CI, Branch — contain no focusable element (`:114-118`), so on a viewport
narrow enough to trigger the overflow there is no keyboard action that brings them into view.
On the `<h1>`/`<h2>`/`<h3>` structure the page otherwise gets right, this is the one gap.

Also missing: with several tables per page carrying identical `<th>` text (Flags, PR, Author,
Age, Review, CI, Branch), nothing distinguishes them to a screen reader's table list. The
`<h2>`/`<h3>` above each one is the only cue, and it is not programmatically associated.

## Impact

Failing scenario: a keyboard-only user opens `/api/github/open-pull-requests.html` on a phone
or a narrow window. Seven columns overflow. They Tab through the PR links fine, but the CI and
Branch columns — the two that say whether a PR is actionable, and the reason the page exists —
are unreachable. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1 (Keyboard, Level A) is not met for that content.

## Fix

Make the scroll container focusable and name it. Both changes are on the same element:

```csharp
private static void AppendTable(StringBuilder builder, IReadOnlyList<PullRequestItem> pullRequests, string label)
{
    // tabindex="0" so a keyboard user can scroll the overflow: columns past PR hold no
    // focusable content, so without it Author..Branch are unreachable on a narrow viewport.
    builder.Append("<div class=\"table-wrap\" tabindex=\"0\" role=\"region\" aria-label=\"")
        .Append(Encode(label))
        .Append("\">\n<table>\n<thead>\n<tr>");
    ...
}
```

Callers already hold the right label: the group title at `:60` and the dependency-group name at
`:68`. Add a matching focus style so the focused region is visible:

```css
.table-wrap:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #1a73e8; outline-offset: 2px; }
```

## Resolution
Each table-wrap now carries tabindex=0, role=region and an aria-label naming its group, plus a focus-visible outline. Covered by Format_makes_each_scrolling_table_keyboard_reachable_and_named.
title: The HTML table's horizontal scroll container is not keyboard-reachable (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1)

## Problem

The cache table is created with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and nothing records which schema
version a given file holds. `IF NOT EXISTS` is exactly the wrong primitive for an evolving
schema: against a file created by an older build it does nothing and reports success, leaving
the process running on a table it believes it just defined.

Because every operation fails open, the resulting breakage is permanent and silent — the same
mode as the deleted-file finding on this file, reached by a different route.

## Evidence

`src/GhPrApi/Caching/SqliteDistributedCache.cs:52-61`:

```csharp
command.CommandText = """
    PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS cache (
        key        TEXT    PRIMARY KEY,
        value      BLOB    NOT NULL,
        expires_at INTEGER NOT NULL
    );
    CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_cache_expires_at ON cache (expires_at);
    """;
```

No `PRAGMA user_version`, no version column, no migration step anywhere in the file.

The project already versions its cache at the *value* level and understands why —
`src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:56` and `:129`:

```csharp
$"listing:v1:{owner}"
$"status:v1:{pullRequest.RepositoryNameWithOwner}#{pullRequest.Number}@{pullRequest.HeadRefOid}"
```

Those `v1` markers exist so a changed payload shape cannot be read back as the old one. The
container that holds them has no equivalent.

The file is explicitly designed to outlive the process — README.md:168: "The second tier is a
SQLite file at `GitHub:CachePath`, so cached work survives a restart or redeploy", with
`compose.yml` mounting a named volume and the Dockerfile declaring `VOLUME ["/data"]`. So an
upgraded binary meeting a previous release's file is the *normal* deployment path, not an edge
case.

## Impact

Failing scenario: a later change adds a column — say `created_at` for cache statistics, or a
`schema` discriminator. The new build starts against the volume written by the previous
release. `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` sees the table and returns success. Every `INSERT`
naming the new column then raises `SQLITE_ERROR: table cache has no column named created_at`,
which the fail-open catch at `:116` swallows and logs as a warning.

Result: the service runs, serves correct data, and the durable tier is dead — every redeploy
pays a full cold fetch, GitHub quota consumption rises to the uncached rate, and the only
symptom is one warning line per cache operation. The `expires_at`-only design means there is
not even a stale-data symptom to notice.

## Fix

Stamp and check a version. `PRAGMA user_version` is free, needs no extra table, and the whole
migration policy for a *cache* is "throw it away":

```csharp
private const int SchemaVersion = 1;

// A cache file outlives the binary that wrote it (VOLUME ["/data"], by design). CREATE TABLE
// IF NOT EXISTS silently accepts an older shape, and every write then fails into the fail-open
// catch -- a permanently dead tier with no symptom but log noise. The file is disposable, so a
// version mismatch drops the table rather than migrating it.
using (var versionCommand = connection.CreateCommand())
{
    versionCommand.CommandText = "PRAGMA user_version;";
    var found = Convert.ToInt32(versionCommand.ExecuteScalar(), CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    if (found != 0 && found != SchemaVersion)
    {
        using var dropCommand = connection.CreateCommand();
        dropCommand.CommandText = "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cache;";
        dropCommand.ExecuteNonQuery();
    }
}
```

then append `PRAGMA user_version = 1;` to the existing DDL batch. Bumping `SchemaVersion`
becomes the entire migration procedure for any future shape change. Add a test that writes a
file, mutates its `user_version`, constructs a new cache over it, and asserts a round trip
still works.

## Resolution
Schema writes PRAGMA user_version = 1; a differing non-zero version drops the table. Covered by A_file_from_a_different_schema_version_is_discarded_rather_than_reused and The_schema_version_written_matches_the_one_checked.
title: The durable cache table carries no schema version, so any future column change silently bricks existing cache files

## Problem

`IPullRequestReportService` exists to be substituted. Nothing substitutes it. It has exactly
one implementation, no test fake, and no second consumer — it is pure indirection between the
endpoint handlers and the single class they call.

## Evidence

Every reference in the repository:

```text
$ grep -rn 'IPullRequestReportService' --include='*.cs' src tests
src/GhPrApi/Services/PullRequestReportService.cs:11:  public sealed class PullRequestReportService : IPullRequestReportService
src/GhPrApi/Services/IPullRequestReportService.cs:5:   public interface IPullRequestReportService
src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:83:                             builder.Services.AddScoped<IPullRequestReportService, PullRequestReportService>();
src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:181:                            IPullRequestReportService reports,
src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:202:                            IPullRequestReportService reports,
src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:212:                            IPullRequestReportService reports,
src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:239:                            IPullRequestReportService reports,
```

One implementer, one registration, four handler parameters. No test implements it:
`PullRequestReportServiceTests:211` constructs the concrete `PullRequestReportService`
directly, and `EndpointTests:293-294` substitutes one layer deeper —
`services.RemoveAll<IGitHubGraphQlClient>()` — because that is where the seam actually is.

The contrast makes the point: `IGitHubGraphQlClient` has two independent test doubles
(`EndpointTests.FakeGitHubGraphQlClient`, `PullRequestReportServiceTests.FakeGitHubGraphQlClient`)
and is genuinely earning its keep. `IPullRequestReportService` has none.

Registering the concrete class works identically — minimal-API handler parameters resolve from
DI by type, and `AddScoped<PullRequestReportService>()` satisfies a `PullRequestReportService`
parameter exactly as the interface does today.

## Impact

No runtime defect; the cost is maintenance. Two files must move in lockstep for every signature
change, and a reader tracing `reports.GetOpenPullRequestsAsync` from `Program.cs` lands on an
interface declaration rather than the implementation. The interface also advertises a seam that
does not exist — the next person adding a test will reasonably try to fake it, discover the
real seam is `IGitHubGraphQlClient`, and have wasted the detour.

## Fix

Delete `src/GhPrApi/Services/IPullRequestReportService.cs`, drop the base type from
`PullRequestReportService`, and change the four handler parameters plus the registration:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddScoped<PullRequestReportService>();
```

Tests need no change: both existing suites already bypass this interface.

If it should stay instead — e.g. an in-memory or replay implementation is genuinely planned —
say so in a comment on the interface, so the next audit does not re-derive that it is unused.

## Resolution
Interface deleted; the concrete PullRequestReportService is registered and injected directly. No test needed changing.
title: IPullRequestReportService is an interface with one implementation and no test double

## Problem

`/openapi/v1.json` is a published contract — README.md:217-219 lists it as an endpoint. Its
description of the `format` parameter names three accepted values. The endpoint accepts four.
The one it omits is the short alias people are most likely to reach for.

## Evidence

The published summary — `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:132`:

```csharp
.WithSummary("Lists currently open pull requests across public, non-archived GitHub repositories owned by the configured account. Format via ?format=json|markdown|html, defaults to json.")
```

What the parser accepts — `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:226-232`:

```csharp
return format.Trim().ToUpperInvariant() switch
{
    "JSON" => ResponseFormat.Json,
    "MARKDOWN" or "MD" => ResponseFormat.Markdown,
    "HTML" => ResponseFormat.Html,
    _ => null,
};
```

`md` is a first-class value, not an undocumented accident: README.md:74 lists it —
"`json`, `markdown`, `md`, or `html`" — and `EndpointTests:24` asserts it works:

```csharp
[InlineData("/api/github/open-pull-requests?format=md", "text/markdown")]
```

So three sources say four values and the machine-readable one says three.

## Impact

Failing scenario: a client is generated from `/openapi/v1.json`, or a developer reads it
instead of the README (the reasonable move — it is the machine-readable contract). They
conclude `md` is unsupported and either write `markdown` everywhere or, worse, treat an
existing `?format=md` call site as a bug and "fix" it.

Low cost, but it is a divergence in the one artifact whose entire job is to be authoritative,
and the codebase otherwise keeps README, tests and implementation in step.

## Fix

One word, in `src/GhPrApi/Program.cs:132`:

```csharp
.WithSummary("Lists currently open pull requests across public, non-archived GitHub repositories owned by the configured account. Format via ?format=json|markdown|md|html, defaults to json.")
```

`EndpointTests.OpenApi_document_generates_and_describes_every_route` already fetches the
document; extend it to assert the summary lists every value `ParseFormat` accepts, so the two
cannot drift again.

## Resolution
OpenAPI summary and the 400 problem detail both list format=md.
title: The OpenAPI summary omits format=md, a value the endpoint accepts and README documents
429 responses carry no Retry-After, on a limiter one caller can exhaust for everyone

## Problem

`src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj` declares both `SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlite3` and
`SQLitePCLRaw.core` at 3.0.5. The `core` declaration is redundant: `bundle_e_sqlite3`
already brings `core` at exactly 3.0.5 through its own dependency chain, so removing the
explicit entry changes nothing about what is restored.

Class: redundant manifest declaration (a duplicate-dependency variant, where the duplicate
is between a direct entry and the transitive it already receives).

## Evidence

**Manifest** — `src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj:26-27`

```xml
<PackageReference Include="SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlite3" Version="3.0.5" />
<PackageReference Include="SQLitePCLRaw.core" Version="3.0.5" />
```

**Lockfile** — `src/GhPrApi/packages.lock.json` currently records both as `Direct`.

**Usage scan** — neither package is referenced from source. Both are declared purely to pin
a transitive version:

```text
$ grep -rn --include='*.cs' -E 'SQLitePCL|Batteries_V2' src/ tests/
(no matches)
```

That is a legitimate reference form for NuGet, so neither is an unused-dependency. The
question is only whether the `core` entry does any work.

**Proof that it does not.** Removing the `core` line and re-running
`dotnet restore --force-evaluate` resolves the family identically:

```text
SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlite3: 3.0.5  (Direct)
SQLitePCLRaw.config.e_sqlite3: 3.0.5  (Transitive)
SQLitePCLRaw.core:             3.0.5  (Transitive)
SQLitePCLRaw.provider.e_sqlite3: 3.0.5 (Transitive)
```

`core` still lands on 3.0.5 via bundle -> config -> provider -> core. The declaration was
reverted after the check; the working tree is unchanged.

## Impact

Low, and partly defensible. The cost is a manifest entry that implies a constraint it is not
providing, plus one extra package Dependabot will open independent bump PRs for. Against
that, an explicit floor does guard against a future `bundle_e_sqlite3` release lowering its
transitive floor on `core` — and this repository has already been bitten once by a
transitive (GHSA-2m69-gcr7-jv3q), which is why the pins exist at all.

So this is a judgement call, not a defect: keep it as deliberate belt-and-braces, or drop it
as noise.

## Fix

Removal is behaviour-affecting in principle and is not applied automatically. If the entry
should go, delete `src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj:27`:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="SQLitePCLRaw.core" Version="3.0.5" />
```

then run `dotnet restore src/GhPrApi/GhPrApi.csproj --force-evaluate` and commit the
regenerated `packages.lock.json`.

If it should stay, extend the existing comment above the block to say the `core` entry is a
deliberate floor guard rather than a required pin, so the next reader does not have to
re-derive that it is redundant today.

## Resolution
Took the finding's documented alternative: kept the pin and extended the csproj comment to record that SQLitePCLRaw.core is redundant today and retained deliberately as a floor guard, so the next reader need not re-derive it.
title: SQLitePCLRaw.core is declared explicitly but resolves identically without it
